sens: That which boils, that is at a very high temperature
Passionate, fervent, full of zeal
G2200.detail:
1. In the literal sense, boiling describes something that is at a very high temperature, like water that is boiling. It is the most concrete physical image of the word: something very hot, trembling with energy.

2. In a figurative sense, boiling characterizes a person or an attitude full of passion and zeal. Revelation uses it to describe the spiritual warmth of a church: to be boiling is to be fervent in faith, burning with love for God. Conversely, to be lukewarm (Revelation 3:15-16) is to be without passion, without conviction, which provokes divine disgust.
G2200.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to boil." The basic image is that of a liquid that boils, trembling under the effect of intense heat. This concrete image naturally extends to the spiritual to evoke intense passion, a fervor that ignites.
G2200.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, in verses 15 and 16 of Revelation 3. These two occurrences are found in the message addressed to the church of Laodicea. Jesus criticizes this church not for being openly hostile or lukewarm, but for lacking spiritual fervor. The contrast of the passage is clear: Jesus would prefer a church that is either "cold" (openly hostile) or "boiling" (passionate and zealous) rather than simply lukewarm. This usage is entirely metaphorical: it does not speak of physical temperature, but of the intensity of devotion and love for God.
G2200.portee: This word reminds the believer that God desires a living and passionate faith, not a dull and unconvincing adherence. Being a Christian is not about occupying a lukewarm place in the church, but burning with love and zeal for the Lord. The word invites one to examine their heart: where is my spiritual fervor?

sens: A team of two work animals joined together to pull
A set of two identical or complementary things
G2201.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a team: two animals (oxen, horses, etc.) tied together by a yoke to pull a plow or vehicle. When the man in Luke 14:19 says, "I have bought five pairs of oxen," he refers to five teams, meaning ten oxen in total, paired for work.
2. More broadly, the word designates two similar things or things that go together: a pair of turtledoves or young pigeons (Luke 2:24), two birds offered together in sacrifice. The image of the yoke remains present: it is the idea of two units linked, forming a functional whole.
G2201.origine: The word comes from the verb "to yoke" (ζεύγνυμι). In biblical Hebrew, it primarily translates צֶמֶד (tsémèd), which has the same meaning: a yoke or a pair of work animals. The basic image is that of the bond that unites two things to make a functional whole.
G2201.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke. First in the literal sense: the five pairs of oxen in Luke 14:19, which a guest has bought and wants to check that they are working well (context of a parable about refusals to follow Jesus). Then in the extended sense: the two birds in Luke 2:24, presented at the Temple during Mary's purification after Jesus' birth, according to Levitical law. In both cases, the word emphasizes that the two elements form a unity: two animals working together, two birds offered together.
G2201.portee: This word reminds us that in Scripture, two things are often linked to form a functional or ritual whole. For the believer, it is an invitation to see how the biblical yoke — like that of the oxen or the birds — speaks of order, harmony, and working together. It is also a detail that grounds the Gospel narratives in concrete life and Jewish laws: Mary was not wealthy; she offered the two turtledoves, not a lamb.

sens: Link used to hold two elements together
Chain or rope connecting the rudder to the ship
The crossbar of a double rudder
G2202.detail: 1. The word primarily designates any link or attachment intended to join two things together. It is the general idea of what unites or connects distinct objects. 2. In the specifically maritime context, it refers to the rope or chain that secures the rudder to the ship and allows for its control. In Acts 27:40, the captain of the ship caught in the storm orders to release these attachments of the rudders to try to steer the boat differently and bring it closer to shore. 3. More technically, it designates the crossbar that connects the two rudders of a double rudder, an essentially mechanical part of the ship.
G2202.origine: The word comes from the Greek root *zeug-* which means "to join" or "to yoke" — it is found in the word *zeugma* (yoke, junction). The adjective *zeuktèrios* literally means "suitable for joining." The form *zeuktèria* specifically designates an attachment or link, and in maritime terms, the system of ropes or bars that unite the parts of the rudder. This word does not appear anywhere else in the Bible.
G2202.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: Acts 27:40, during Paul's shipwreck on the way to Malta. Luke describes the desperate maneuvers of the sailors in the storm: they throw the anchor into the sea and release the attachments of the rudders, seeking to change strategy to save the ship. The context is that of ancient navigation and the practical techniques of sailors. Paul, a prisoner on board, observes these actions that testify to the professionalism and resourcefulness of the sailors in the face of imminent disaster.
G2202.portee: This technical detail of the shipwreck narrative reminds the reader that God also acts in the concrete and material realities of our lives — here, a storm at sea, ropes, decisions of sailors. Luke does not hesitate to note the precise actions of experienced men, which heightens the reality of danger and, by contrast, the power of the divine deliverance that will follow.

sens: The king of the gods in Greco-Roman mythology
The deity to whom pagans offered worship and sacrifices
G2203.detail:
1. Jupiter (or Zeus in Greek) is the supreme god of the Greco-Roman pantheon: he is the most powerful deity in the religious beliefs of the Greeks and Romans. When the inhabitants of Lystra see Paul heal a crippled man, they are so struck that they identify Barnabas as Jupiter and Paul as Mercury (Acts 14:12), so much does the miracle seem superhuman.
2. It is a living deity of public worship: pagans dedicated temples, priests to him, and offered animal sacrifices. After believing that Paul was Mercury, "the priest of Jupiter, whose temple was at the entrance of the city, brought bulls with ribbons to the gates" to sacrifice to what he believed was a visit from the gods (Acts 14:13).
G2203.origine: Zeus is the Greek name for the king of the gods; Jupiter is the Latin name. This word designates in the Bible the central deity of Greco-Roman paganism to which non-believers render worship. The Greek text uses the nominative Ζεύς and also employs declined forms like Δία (accusative) to fit the grammatical context of the narrative.
G2203.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 14 during Paul and Barnabas's visit to Lystra, a city in Galatia. The usage shows how the Greeks of this region identified gods with superhuman powers: the healing miracle appears as proof of divine presence. Paul and Barnabas refuse these divine honors, marking the contrast between idol worship and the worship of the true God. This is the only point where the New Testament explicitly names a pagan deity worshiped.
G2203.portee: This mention reminds the Christian reader that ancient paganism was rich in alluring cults and vibrant religious practices, but that these gods were merely human inventions. It also shows how the apostles firmly rejected any divine honor, refusing to be treated as gods, and proclaimed the one true God. It is a silent warning against idolatry in all its forms.

sens: To boil, to be burning (in the literal sense)
To burn with an intense feeling (anger, love, zeal)
To be ardent, passionate in the service of God
G2204.detail:
1. The word literally describes water that is boiling or heat that is burning — it is an image of nature that is in a state of agitation.
2. Figuratively, it denotes a heart that burns with a powerful feeling: rising anger, consuming love, inflamed zeal. It is an inner fire that stirs the whole person.
3. In the Christian life, it characterizes one whose spirit is ablaze for God. In Acts 18:25, Apollos is described as 'fervent in spirit' as he accurately proclaims Jesus; in Romans 12:11, Paul urges believers to be 'fervent in spirit' in their service to the Lord, in contrast to laziness and lukewarmness.
G2204.origine: The Greek word zeō comes from a root that depicts boiling, bubbling. It simply images the natural spectacle of water boiling under heat. The metaphor then extends to the passions and dispositions of the soul — what is burning outside becomes the symbol of what burns inside. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, it often translates verbs like rouah (to boil) or ratah (to foam), which are also drawn from the image of fire.
G2204.emploi: The verb zeō appears twice in the New Testament, always in the form of the adjectival participle 'fervent'. Acts 18:25 applies it to Apollos, an eloquent man rich in knowledge of Scripture, whose heart burns with zeal for Jesus despite an incomplete understanding. Romans 12:11 uses it as a direct exhortation: Paul commands the Christians of the community in Rome to be 'fervent in spirit', that is, to serve the Lord with a lively passion and without slackness. The context shows that it is a moral quality — the opposite of laziness — that must be cultivated in one's faith life.
G2204.portee: This word tells us that the Christian faith must never become lukewarm or routine. It demands fervor, passion, a surge of the heart. To be 'fervent in spirit' is to refuse spiritual mediocrity and to offer God a heart that burns, not a cold heart. It is a call to authenticity and intensity in the service of God.

sens: Passionate ardor for a cause, a person, or a mission
Jealous vigilance, possessive attachment towards someone or something
Envious anger, desire to compete with or harm others
Religious fervor, intensive devotion to the Law or to faith
G2205.detail:
1. Zeal is a passionate ardor that drives someone to act vigorously for a cause they love. It is a driving force, a burning energy that consumes the one who feels it. For example, the disciples remember that Jesus' zeal for the house of God 'consumes' him (John 2:17), like a fire that burns within. Similarly, Paul boasts of the zeal of the Corinthians for giving (2 Corinthians 9:2).

2. Zeal can also express jealous vigilance, a possessive attachment towards someone. Paul speaks of the zeal that God has for His people, comparable to that of a husband jealous for his wife (2 Corinthians 11:2): it is a love that jealously watches over what belongs to Him.

3. This jealousy can become negative and turn into malicious envy, a desire to compete or harm others. Jealousy appears alongside quarrels and hatred as a poison that divides communities (Romans 13:13; 1 Corinthians 3:3), manifesting carnal weakness.

4. In a religious context, zeal refers to fervor or intensive devotion to the Law or to faith. Paul recounts that he persecuted the Church 'according to the zeal' he had for the Law (Philippians 3:6), meaning with a misdirected religious passion. This zeal can be noble when based on true knowledge, but it can also be blind and destructive.
G2205.origine: The Greek word zèlos (ζῆλος) comes from a root that expresses the idea of boiling or smoking, evoking ardor that quickly rises into flames. In Hebrew, the parallel word is qinah (קִנְאָה), which means passionate jealousy, possessive love, or zealous vigilance — a passion that is attributed to God Himself as an expression of His love for His people. The word also appears in the family of the Greek verb zéloô (zêloô), which means 'to be jealous of' or 'to envy'. This common root shows that zeal and jealousy are two sides of the same passion: positive when it protects what one loves, negative when it degenerates into envy.
G2205.emploi: The word zeal appears 16 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Pauline epistles. It is translated as 'zeal' when it describes noble ardor, devoted to a good cause, and as 'jealousy' when it expresses malicious envy or possessive jealousy. In a positive context, Paul praises the zeal of the Corinthians for sharing (2 Corinthians 9:2) and commends Titus for the zeal he shows (2 Corinthians 7:7); he speaks of God's zeal for His people (2 Corinthians 11:2). In a negative context, zeal becomes jealousy: it is a work of the flesh that divides the Church (Galatians 5:20), it appears alongside quarrels (Romans 13:13; 1 Corinthians 3:3; 2 Corinthians 12:20), and the Jews are filled with jealousy against Paul and his message (Acts 13:45). The context thus allows us to discern whether zeal is a force for life or a poison of death.
G2205.portee: The word zeal reminds the Christian reader of the importance of passion and commitment, but also the danger of allowing that passion to degenerate into envy and rivalry. Paul shows that misdirected zeal, even if sincere, can lead to the persecution of the Church (Philippians 3:6). The solution is not to extinguish passion, but to redirect it: to seek zeal for good works, for the growth of the body of Christ, and for the love of the Lord, rather than to be consumed by envy of others. This is how zeal becomes a spiritual virtue in the service of God.

sens: To burn with jealousy or envy towards someone
To desire something intensely, to aspire to it eagerly
To seek to obtain or imitate with eagerness
To be filled with passionate zeal
G2206.detail:
1. To be jealous means to burn with envy towards someone who possesses what one covets. The patriarchs were jealous of Joseph because he was Jacob's favorite (Acts 7:9); the Jews in Acts 17:5 became jealous of Paul and Silas because the crowd was pressing around them. It is an emotion that divides and drives one to act against the one envied.
2. To aspire or desire ardently means to actively seek, to covet something with passion. Paul tells the church in Corinth: "Desire the best gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:31), not with destructive envy, but with a holy desire to receive what is best to serve God. It is the same verb, but directed towards what is good.
3. To seek to imitate or possess in a movement of eagerness: Paul writes that he urges the Galatians with zeal to seek spiritual gifts, also to put them to use (Galatians 4:17). The fervor of zeal can be good or bad depending on its direction.
4. The context of passionate zeal appears when Paul says that the Galatians must be "zealous" for good (Galatians 4:18: "It is good to be zealous"). It is an intensity of heart that, when well-directed, becomes pious fervor.
G2206.origine: The verb comes from a root that expresses heat, ardent passion. It is formed from the Greek noun zèlos (ζῆλος), zeal — that is, intense ardor, burning envy. In Hebrew, the verb קָנָא (qana) carries the same double meaning: destructive jealousy (God himself is "jealous" — in the sense of jealously protecting — His people) and passionate desire. The Greek word translates the Hebrew in the Greek Old Testament.
G2206.emploi: This verb appears 10 times in the New Testament. Its uses are clearly divided into two groups: first, negative jealousy, the consuming envy (Acts 7:9; 17:5: the patriarchs, the Jews jealous of Paul) and 1 Corinthians 13:4 where Paul affirms that love is not envious. Then, the positive aspiration for good: Paul encourages the Corinthians to aspire to spiritual gifts, especially prophecy (1 Corinthians 12:31; 14:1; 14:39). In Galatians 4:17-18, Paul speaks of the zeal that one has for him and zeal for good, showing that the same word can denote a passion directed towards God or turned towards evil. The context determines whether zeal is a virtue or a vice.
G2206.portee: This word teaches the Christian the power of desire that governs the heart. Jealousy and envy are destructive forces that divide the Church and lead to sin (Acts 17:5); but this same inner fire, directed towards the gifts of the Spirit and towards God, becomes a holy fervor. The Christian is called not to extinguish his zeal, but to transform it: to aspire to the best, to seek the spiritual gifts that edify the Church rather than coveting the glory of others.

sens: One who is passionately attached to the law or a cause
A member of the political and religious party of the Zealots in the first century
The apostle Simon, called the Zealot
G2207.detail:
1. The word designates someone who ardently defends a cause or a law — it is a zealous admirer, full of enthusiasm. Peter speaks of Christians "zealous for good works" (1 Peter 3:13), meaning ardently committed to doing good. Paul, before his conversion, was a passionate zealot for the Jewish tradition: "I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers" (Galatians 1:14).
2. At the time of the New Testament, the Zealots formed a political and religious party radically opposed to Roman control over Israel. They preached armed revolt to regain independence. The disciples in Jerusalem included "many thousands of Jews […] all zealous for the law" (Acts 21:20), a term designating both the current of thought and the men who carried it.
3. Simon, one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, received the nickname "the Zealot" (Luke 6:15), which meant either that he had once belonged to the Zealot party or that he was known for his ardent zeal.
G2207.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb zēloō ("to be zealous, to be jealous"), itself formed from zēlos ("zeal, ardor, jealousy"). The latter often translates the Hebrew word qinnâ, meaning "jealousy" or "ardor" — notably the ardor of God for His rights and honor. In the Greek Old Testament, it is written that God Himself is a jealous God (zealous), Exodus 20:5. The word thus has a deep religious root: it designates a passion for what is considered just or sacred.
G2207.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament. Paul first uses it to describe his own past: "I was zealous for the traditions" (Galatians 1:14) and "I was zealous for God" (Acts 22:3). He then uses it to exhort Christians to this same zeal, but directed towards good: "zealous for spiritual gifts" (1 Corinthians 14:12), "zealous for good works" (Titus 2:14, 1 Peter 3:13). Acts 21:20 places the word in a political context: the Jewish disciples are "zealous for the law" in the sense of the Zealot party. Finally, Simon receives this nickname three times (Luke 6:15, Acts 1:13) as an identifier among the apostles.
G2207.portee: This word reminds the reader that zeal is not bad in itself — it is an ardor, a passion for what one believes to be right. Paul had it, but he redirected it after his encounter with Jesus, from defending traditions to loving Christ. For today's Christian, the Zealot Simon and the example of Paul invite us to examine our own zeal: is it in service of God and the gospel, or is it still imprisoned in human structures that resist God?

sens: member of the Jewish political and religious movement opposed to Roman domination
by extension, a passionate supporter of a cause
G2208.detail:
1. The Zealot is a member of the Jewish movement that emerged in the first century, characterized by an ardent attachment to the Law of God and active resistance against Roman occupation. This term historically designates the Jewish revolutionaries who refused to recognize Roman authority in the Holy Land. Simon, one of Jesus' apostles, is identified as "Simon the Zealot" in the lists of disciples (Acts 1:13), which likely indicates his affiliation with this movement before becoming a disciple.
2. Figuratively, a zealot is a person animated by intense zeal, an ardent passion for a cause or ideal. Although this meaning is not explicitly developed in the New Testament, the term carries the idea of deep conviction and determination.
G2208.origine: The Greek word zēlōtēs comes from zēlos, which means "zeal" or "jealous ardor." It is formed on the model of other agent nouns in -tēs (like "poiètès," poet). Zealotry was a specifically Jewish movement of the first century, imbued with the desire to maintain the purity of the Jewish faith and to liberate Israel from foreign domination. The name reflects the characteristic ardor of its members.
G2208.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in identical contexts: the lists of the twelve apostles. In Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13, Simon is referred to as "Simon the Zealot." This designation distinguishes him from another apostle named Simon Peter, and it reveals the historical origin of this apostle before his calling by Jesus. The New Testament context thus makes Zealotry a concrete historical fact: it was a recognizable and well-defined movement in the Judaism of the time, notable enough to serve as an identifying label.
G2208.portee: The fact that Jesus called Simon, a Zealot, to be an apostle shows that He came to seek men even in their most ardent convictions, including among revolutionaries. It also reveals the diversity of the backgrounds of His disciples: some were tax collectors, others were zealous nationalists. Simon's conversion suggests a transformation: his zeal for God, once channeled through political struggle, was redirected towards the service of the Kingdom of God inaugurated by Jesus. This is an invitation for the reader to consider how God can transform and redirect our passion.

sens: material damage or harm
injury, detriment to what one possesses
relinquishment of a good to acquire a better one
G2209.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a concrete damage, a material loss: in Acts 27:10 and 27:21, Paul warns the sailors that the voyage will result in a loss, a damage to the cargo and the ship. It is the ruin of precious things.

2. More broadly, it refers to any injury, any detriment to what one possesses or to what one is: a loss of money, freedom, or security. The word suggests being deprived of something of value.

3. In Philippians 3:7 and 3:8, Paul radicalizes this meaning: he calls the relinquishment of all the goods and advantages of his former life (advantages of birth, education, status) a "loss" because he considers them worthless compared to the knowledge of Christ. This is not a loss suffered, but a willingly accepted sacrifice, a joyful sacrifice.
G2209.origine: The Greek ζημία comes from a root meaning "to diminish" or "to cut down." It is the opposite of κέρδος ("gain"), as shown in the passages from Philippians where Paul contrasts loss and gain. The Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew עָנַשׁ ("to punish") and its forms with this word: loss is often a punishment or deprivation.
G2209.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, concentrated in two very different contexts. In Acts (27:10, 27:21), Paul uses it to describe the danger of a sea crossing: "loss" threatens the ship, the cargo, and lives. In Philippians (3:7, 3:8), it is a language of relinquishment: Paul lists all his former religious and social privileges and then calls them "loss" in light of Christ. This passage shows how the same word can evoke both a real dispossession and a deliberate choice to abandon what seemed good to find something better.
G2209.portee: For the Christian reader, this entry invites meditation on what Paul teaches: there is a loss that destroys (that of shipwreck), but also a loss that saves (that of the voluntary relinquishment of what separates us from Christ). It frees from the fear of a true loss accepted to follow Jesus.

sens: To suffer a loss, to be deprived of something
To lose one's life, one's soul, to be separated from it forever
To lose a reward, to be frustrated of it
To be damaged, to suffer harm
G2210.detail:
1. To lose means to be deprived of something one possessed: it is to suffer a loss. Paul says in Philippians 3:8 that he has "renounced everything" (literally, considers everything as loss) to gain Christ — he chose to abandon his human advantages.
2. To lose one's soul or life is the most serious issue: it is to lose it eternally, to be separated from God forever. Jesus asks three times (Matthew 16:26, Mark 8:36, Luke 9:25): what does it profit a man to gain the whole world if he loses his soul?
3. To lose a reward means to be deprived of it on the day of judgment: in 1 Corinthians 3:15, the one whose work does not endure will lose his reward, although he himself will be saved.
4. To lose can also mean to suffer damage or harm: in 2 Corinthians 7:9, Paul speaks of "receiving no harm from us," meaning no injury or detriment.
G2210.origine: The word comes from the root zémia (zémia) which denotes a loss, damage, or lack. It is a concrete word that primarily evokes material damage. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb "anash" (to punish, to damage). The verb in the passive form literally means "to be damaged" or "to receive harm," hence the meaning of "to lose" or "to suffer a loss."
G2210.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament. Three occurrences in the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) report Jesus' teaching on the ultimate risk of losing one's soul. Jesus poses a rhetorical question to show the absurdity of sacrificing one's eternity for worldly goods. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 3:15 for the loss of a heavenly reward (not of salvation itself), and in 2 Corinthians 7:9 for moral or spiritual damage. In Philippians 3:8, Paul expresses his voluntary decision to consider everything as loss — he renounces the legal advantages of Judaism for the excellence of knowing Christ.
G2210.portee: This word shows how seriously Jesus takes each person's eternity: there is no possible compromise between gaining the world and losing one's soul. He invites the believer to rethink their priorities: what is truly worth it? For the disciple, it is a call to the voluntary abandonment of false treasures (like Paul) to obtain the only treasure that matters — the relationship with Christ. It is also a warning about the eternal consequences of our choices.

sens: A Christian mentioned in the epistle to Titus
G2211.detail: Zenas is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Titus 3:13. He is a believer whom Paul recommends to receive help and hospitality, along with Apollos, when they travel.
G2211.origine: The name Zenas is the shortened form of the Greek Zénodore, which literally means "gift of Zeus" (Zén- referring to Zeus, and -dore meaning gift). It is a common Greek name, borne by several ancient figures.
G2211.emploi: Zenas appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 3:13. Paul asks Titus to "carefully send Zenas, who is learned in the law." This brief mention tells us that he was known to Titus and Paul, that he possessed knowledge of the Mosaic Law, and that he was traveling with Apollos. He seems to be a trustworthy collaborator in the apostolic work.

sens: To seek something or someone in order to find them
To pursue someone with the intent to harm
To desire to obtain something, to strive to achieve it
To demand, to ask as a condition
To question, to examine through reflection
G2212.detail:
1. The most common meaning: to traverse, explore a space to discover what one desires. Jesus says, "Knock, and it will be opened to you; for everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds" (Matthew 7:7-8). The farmer who comes to seek fruit from his fig tree (Luke 13:6) embodies this concrete movement of investigation.

2. To pursue someone to do them harm: Herod seeks the young child Jesus to destroy him (Matthew 2:13), and the Jews seek to kill Jesus (John 7:1). This is a hostile quest, a hunt.

3. To desire, to aspire to, to strive to obtain: "Seek first the kingdom of God" (Matthew 6:33) means to make this kingdom your priority, your passionate pursuit. It is to aim for something of value.

4. To formally demand or request, as a condition or proof: "This generation seeks a sign" (Luke 11:29), meaning it claims, it asks as justification.

5. To question in order to understand, to reflect on something: "They were questioning among themselves who would be the greatest" (Luke 9:46, implicit) — to examine, to debate internally.
G2212.origine: The Greek verb zēteō comes from a root evoking the activity of searching, of questing. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it primarily translates the Hebrew baqash ("to seek," "to ask"), which carries the idea of going forth in quest with determination. The word can also translate darash ("to seek," "to consult"). The family of the verb includes zétèsis (the search, the investigation) and zètètès (the one who seeks). The underlying image is that of an active quest, a voluntary pursuit.
G2212.emploi: The verb zēteō appears 116 times in the New Testament and is central in the Gospel of John (over 30 occurrences). It is also very frequent in the Synoptics. The most common context is the search for Jesus: crowds seek him to follow or speak to him (John 7:11), authorities seek to seize or kill him (Mark 12:12, John 7:1). Jesus uses the word to invite to persistent prayer (Matthew 7:7) and to prioritize the kingdom of God (Matthew 6:33). Sometimes it is a simple request ("Whom are you seeking?" John 18:4), other times a demand or a claim (Luke 11:29). The verb can also carry a moral nuance: seeking one's own glory (John 7:18) or that of God (John 8:50).
G2212.portee: This verb invites the reader to reflect on what they are truly seeking: temporal satisfaction, security, or the kingdom of God? The phrase "Seek first the kingdom of God" (Matthew 6:33) challenges every believer to realign their priorities. The verb also shows that faith is not passive: it requires a search, a conscious quest for God. Finally, by observing how people seek Jesus — to follow him, to judge him, to kill him — we understand that our relationship to Jesus reveals the state of our hearts.

sens: Subject or point on which one inquires or debates
Point of disagreement or dispute between people
Area of controversy or theological and religious debate
G2213.detail:
1. A question is a subject that demands an answer, a point of inquiry: Paul and Barnabas must go up to Jerusalem to "discuss this question" of the requirements of Judaism for converts (Acts 15:2). It is the very content of what is being asked and discussed.
2. A question can also be a point of conflict, a litigated matter that opposes people: when the Roman tribune states that Paul has "committed no crime," but is only "accused concerning questions relating to their law" (Acts 23:29), he distinguishes between true crime and mere dispute over religious points.
3. It often designates a matter of debate or controversy, particularly in religious and theological areas: the Jews of Ephesus have "discussions relating to their religion" with Paul (Acts 25:19), meaning debates about faith and practices.
G2213.origine: The word comes from the root *ζητέω* (zêtéô, "to seek, to search"). A question is fundamentally an ongoing search, something posed to find or clarify. The Hebrew word *דָּרַשׁ* (dâraš, "to seek, to consult, to interpret") corresponds to it in the ancient Greek texts of the Old Testament. The question arises from the human need to understand, to clarify, to debate what is not obvious.
G2213.emploi: The term *zêtêma* appears five times in Acts, always in the speeches of Paul or about him, between chapter 15 and chapter 26. It first designates the major theological question of the Jerusalem assembly: must one observe the Mosaic Law to be a Christian? (Acts 15:2). It then broadens to designate any religious debate: Gallio refuses to judge "discussions about a word, names, and your law" (Acts 18:15). Festus uses it to say that Paul is pursued not for a crime, but for "questions relating to their law" (Acts 23:29; 25:19). Finally, Agrippa acknowledges that Paul knows "their customs and their discussions" (Acts 26:3). The term consistently highlights the theological and not criminal nature of the accusations against Paul.
G2213.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader see how the Gospel has produced authentic questions and debates at the heart of the early Church. Paul does not shy away from questions; he confronts them with intelligence and patience. This word also shows that the Roman authorities distinguished between true crimes and mere religious disputes. For today's Christian, it reminds us that faith raises legitimate questions that deserve to be discussed seriously, without confusion between sincere doubt and bad faith.

sens: Action de chercher, de rechercher
Questionnement, interrogation
Débat, controverse entre personnes
Dispute de mots, querelle stérile
G2214.detail: 1. The basic meaning is the action of seeking or searching for something: it is a quest, an investigation. 2. The word then designates questioning, interrogation — the moment when one asks questions and reflects on something. 3. It takes on the meaning of debate or controversy when two people or groups exchange opposing arguments: this occurs in Jerusalem when a great discussion arises about the circumcision of the Gentiles (Acts 15:7), or when a dispute arises between the disciples of John and a Jew regarding purification (John 3:25). 4. In the pastoral epistles, the word takes on a pejorative connotation: it designates idle, useless, and vain discussions, those arising from pride and seeking only quarrels — like the idle questions and disputes of words that the author rejects (1 Timothy 6:4, 2 Timothy 2:23).
G2214.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to seek" (ζητέω). It retains this basic image: to seek, to investigate, to strive to find. But from seeking, it naturally transitions to discussion, as to discuss is to seek the truth together or to attempt to convince. The form ending in -σις (especially common in classical and late Greek) denotes the action or state. The negative nuance (vain discussion and quarrel) gradually develops in the vocabulary of the New Testament, particularly in Paul.
G2214.emploi: The word appears mainly in Acts and in the pastoral epistles. In Acts, it retains a relative neutrality: it describes real debates, moments of controversy and deliberation (Acts 15:2, 15:7, 25:20), without intrinsic moral value. But in the epistles to Timothy and Titus, the meaning becomes clearly pejorative. Paul instructs Timothy to reject foolish and useless discussions (2 Timothy 2:23), and to guard against a man who has the disease of idle questions and disputes of words (1 Timothy 6:4). This term then designates sterile theological chatter, controversy arising from pride that produces envy, quarrels, and slander — all bad fruits.
G2214.portee: This word teaches the reader an important lesson: one must distinguish between healthy debate (when seeking truth in unity, like the apostles in Jerusalem) and destructive verbal squabbling (when seeking quarrel out of pride). Discussion is good if it aims for clarity and communion; it becomes pernicious when it is merely a dispute of words and a quest for personal victory. It is an invitation to examine our own debates and questions: are we seeking truth and edification, or do we succumb to the sterile pleasure of controversy?

sens: Plante sauvage ressemblant au blé
Mauvaise herbe qu'on sème intentionnellement pour gâcher une récolte
Au sens figuré : les méchants ou les faux croyants au milieu du peuple de Dieu
G2215.detail:
1. The tares are a wild plant, a type of weed that closely resembles wheat when it grows. It can only be distinguished from wheat when it begins to mature (Matthew 13:26). It is a real plant that grows in the fields of the Near East.

2. In Jesus' parable, an enemy deliberately sows tares in a man's wheat field while he sleeps (Matthew 13:25). This is an act of sabotage: destroying someone else's harvest by planting a weed that looks too much like wheat to be uprooted without risk.

3. Jesus uses this image to speak of the wicked mixed among the righteous: the tares represent false believers, people who do evil and live among the people of God, impossible to completely separate at this time (Matthew 13:38, 13:40). At the final harvest, God will separate and burn them.
G2215.origine: The Greek word zizanion comes from Mediterranean popular language and refers to a well-known plant: ryegrass or darnel. In Hebrew and Aramaic, it was called zunim. It is a concrete word that describes a specific botanical reality of the Middle East, and Matthew uses it as is so that his readers recognize the familiar plant they knew.
G2215.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the New Testament, exclusively in Matthew 13 (verses 25, 26, 27, 29, 30, 36, 38, 40), at the heart of the parable of the enemy sower. Jesus first explains the concrete story: an enemy sows tares, the servants notice and want to uproot them, but the master refuses for fear of damaging the wheat. At the harvest, everything will be separated. Then Jesus returns to the spiritual meaning: the tares represent the children of the evil one, the wheat the children of the kingdom. The tares must be gathered and burned at the final judgment.
G2215.portee: This parable teaches Christians that in the earthly Church, good and evil coexist, and it is not our place to judge or separate violently. Only God, at the final harvest, will make this separation. It also invites us to examine our own hearts: are we true wheat, or do we live as tares? It reminds us that true judgment belongs to God alone, and that rushing to judge others can cause us spiritual harm.

sens: fils de Salathiel, ancêtre de Jésus selon la généalogie de Luc
G2216G.detail: 1. Zorobabel is a man mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus according to the Gospel of Luke (Luke 3:27). He appears in this long list of names that traces back from Jesus to Adam, to show that Jesus is truly a son of Israel with deep roots in the history of the chosen people.
G2216G.origine: The name Zorobabel comes from the Hebrew Zerubbabel, which literally means "seed of Babylon." This name was borne by an important historical figure of the Old Testament: the governor of Judah who led the return of the exiles from Babylon and oversaw the reconstruction of the temple after the exile (around 520 BC). The name recalls this crucial period when the people of God, scattered in exile, returned to rebuild.
G2216G.emploi: Zorobabel is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:27, where he appears in the genealogy of Jesus. He is not a character living at the time of Jesus, but a distant ancestor who places Jesus in the continuity of the sacred history of Israel and links him to the promise of restoration of the people after the exile.
G2216G.portee: By placing Zorobabel in the genealogy of Jesus, Luke reminds believers that Jesus is the fulfillment of the promises made to Israel. Zorobabel restored the physical temple; Jesus, in the lineage of this great restorer, comes to restore the entire people. It is an invitation to recognize that God's story has never stopped, even in the worst moments, and that Jesus is its culmination.

sens: Descendant de David et chef de Juda au retour de l'exil à Babylone
Figure généalogique dans la ligne de Jésus
G2216H.detail:
1. Zorobabel is the leader who brought the exiled Jews from Babylon back to Jerusalem and oversaw the reconstruction of the temple. He is an important historical figure in the Old Testament, symbolizing the restoration of Israel after the judgment of exile. Matthew mentions him as an essential link in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:12), specifying that he is the son of Shealtiel and the father of Abiud.

2. In the Gospel, Zorobabel primarily appears as a name in the genealogy: he embodies the continuity of the divine promise made to David, connecting the kings of Judah (before the exile) to the immediate ancestors of Jesus. His name in Matthew's genealogy reminds us that even after the exile and the apparent break in the Davidic monarchy, God preserved his lineage until the coming of the Messiah.
G2216H.origine: Zorobabel comes from the Hebrew זְרֻבָּבֶל (Zerubbabel), which literally means "seed of Babylon" or "born in Babylon." This name reflects his origin: he was born in exile in Babylon and led the return of his people. The name carries within it the hope of return and restoration.
G2216H.emploi: Zorobabel appears twice in the Gospel of Matthew, exclusively in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:12-13). He is listed as the son of Shealtiel and the father of Abiud, forming a link in the chain that traces back to David and descends to Joseph, the legal father of Jesus. The Gospel of Luke also mentions his name in the genealogy it presents (Luke 3:27). These two different genealogies testify to the importance of this figure in the tradition of the Jewish people: Zorobabel, a figure of reconstruction and hope after the exile, is a major witness to God's faithfulness to the house of David and his people.
G2216H.portee: Zorobabel reminds the reader that even in the darkest moments (the exile in Babylon), God never abandons his promises. His presence in the genealogy of Jesus affirms that the Messiah is not a break with Israel's past, but the fulfillment of the covenant made with David. It invites the Christian to recognize the faithfulness and patience of God who, through the generations, leads history toward salvation.

sens: Obscurité complète, absence de lumière
Profondeur ou demeure souterraine sombre
Condition ou état de condamnation et d'éloignement de Dieu
Ignorance spirituelle ou absence de vérité divine
G2217.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the densest physical darkness, one that cannot be pierced by sight — the very image of what is hidden and inaccessible. It is the word the Bible uses to speak of the darkness of Tartarus, the underground region of the dead in Greek mythology, which explains its later metaphorical use.
2. It thus evokes a deep, obscure dwelling, separated from the world of the living and light — a place of detention, confinement. In 2 Peter 2:4, it refers to the "pits of darkness" where God has cast the rebellious angels, chained in waiting for judgment.
3. By extension, the "darkness" becomes the biblical symbol of eternal condemnation and separation from God: it is the fate reserved for those who reject the divine light. In Jude 1:13, "the darkness of the gloom" is reserved eternally for wandering stars — an image of false teachers delivered to judgment.
4. Spiritually, darkness also represents ignorance of the true God and the absence of his revelation: the state of one who lives far from the knowledge of Christ, the Light of the world.
G2217.origine: The Greek word zophos is related to gnophos (thick fog). Its etymology evokes the idea of what envelops, surrounds, and obscures vision. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (Septuagint), it renders the Hebrew araphel, which denotes the darkness of clouds and divine judgment — notably during the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 10:22). The word belongs to the poetic and late vocabulary of Greek, where it carries both a mythological and theological hue.
G2217.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, primarily in the epistles of judgment: Hebrews, 2 Peter, and Jude. In Hebrews 12:18, it is found in the description of the Law at Sinai — the mountain shrouded in darkness where God manifested himself in a frightening way. In 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 1:6, darkness becomes the punishment reserved for fallen angels, chained in obscurity awaiting final judgment. In 2 Peter 2:17 and Jude 1:13, false teachers and wandering stars are also destined for this eternal darkness. The word always emphasizes the idea of separation, judgment, and deprivation of God's presence.
G2217.portee: This word reminds the believer that divine condemnation is not merely an external punishment, but a profound spiritual reality: the total and eternal absence of the face of God, the separation from his light and life. It awakens the conscience to the danger of sin and apostasy. It also invites gratitude for the light offered in Christ, who alone rescues from the power of darkness.

sens: Dispositif en bois reliant deux animaux de trait pour les faire travailler ensemble
Charge ou fardeau imposé à quelqu'un
Assujettissement, servitude ou domination
Instrument pour peser, équilibre des poids
G2218.detail:
1. The yoke is primarily the wooden device placed on the necks of draft animals (oxen, donkeys) to harness them together to a cart or plow. It is an instrument of work and physical constraint.

2. The word then figuratively designates any burden or charge imposed. Jesus invites his disciples to take "his yoke" upon them (Matthew 11:29), this yoke being gentle and his burden light: he speaks of a submission, but one that is kind and lightens the soul.

3. More broadly, the yoke represents servitude and subjugation to an oppressive authority. Peter reproaches the Pharisees for wanting to place "a yoke" on the necks of the disciples, a yoke that no one can bear (Acts 15:10); Paul exhorts the Galatians not to fall back "under the yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1), meaning not to allow themselves to be subjected again to stifling legal obligations.

4. A balance, the instrument that weighs one thing against another to determine equivalence: in Revelation, a rider holds a balance (Revelation 6:5) to measure the prices of wheat and barley.
G2218.origine: The Greek word zugos comes from the verb zeugumi, "to harness" or "to unite." Its primary image is that of harnessing: the yoke connects two animals so they can work in step. In Hebrew, עֹל (ol) carries the same double meaning: both material yoke and figurative servitude. The root evokes the idea of balance and union — hence the secondary transition to the meaning of "balance," an instrument of equilibrium and equal weights.
G2218.emploi: The word yoke appears six times in the New Testament. Jesus uses it twice in Matthew 11 to speak of his yoke as a symbol of joyful and light submission. Peter and Paul use it to denote oppression: Peter opposes the yoke of the Mosaic Law (Acts 15:10), Paul exhorts to reject the yoke of legal slavery (Galatians 5:1) and to respect the masters of those who are "under the yoke of servitude" (1 Timothy 6:1). Only once, in Revelation 6:5, does the word mean "balance," the weighing instrument. The biblical use of the yoke thus nuances: sometimes it is a joyful and light submission, sometimes an oppressive servitude.
G2218.portee: The yoke of Jesus teaches the believer that there is a submission that rests and lightens rather than oppresses. Unlike stifling religious traditions, the yoke of Christ is gentle because it comes with his benevolent presence. Refusing the yoke of servitude (the Law, guilt, legalism) is an affirmation of freedom in Christ. For servants, the text of 1 Timothy invites seeing the yoke as a worldly state to which one can remain dignified and submissive without losing dignity before God.

sens: substance that causes dough to rise
hidden influence that acts gradually
deceptive teaching or false doctrine
concealed hypocrisy
G2219.detail:
1. Leaven is a substance (fermented dough) that is mixed with flour to make bread rise. It is an image of gradual transformation: a small amount transforms the entire dough (1 Corinthians 5:6).
2. This hidden and gradual action of leaven symbolizes any moral influence that works silently from within. Jesus warns His disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees, meaning their negative influence (Matthew 16:6).
3. In this context, leaven specifically refers to the deceptive teaching of religious leaders: the disciples first take it literally, then understand that it refers to their doctrine (Matthew 16:12).
4. By speaking of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, Jesus shows that what acts in secret is their moral falseness (Luke 12:1).
G2219.origine: The Greek word zumē translates two Hebrew words: chametz (unleavened bread) and seor (the leaven itself). These terms describe the natural process of fermentation. Leaven is the fermented dough reserved for the next baking. The image evokes something alive, active, that transmits and transforms.
G2219.emploi: The word appears about 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, and in Paul's letters. It has two distinct uses. First, the literal sense: the parable of the leaven (Matthew 13:33, Luke 13:21) where Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to a small amount of leaven that makes the whole dough rise. Then, the figurative use for evil: Paul uses it for moral impurity in the Church (1 Corinthians 5:6-8), and Jesus warns against the leaven of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Herod (Matthew 16:6, 11, Mark 8:15, Luke 12:1). In all these figurative cases, the idea of gradual contamination prevails.
G2219.portee: Understanding biblical leaven helps the believer grasp two major truths. First, the kingdom of God acts like a small seed that transforms everything from within: faith is not spectacular, but effective. Second, this teaching shows the danger of insidious influences: a false doctrine, hypocrisy, or moral complacency spreads silently within the Christian community. That is why Paul calls to "clean out the old leaven" (1 Corinthians 5:7): vigilance and purity are essential.

sens: Make the dough light and fluffy by incorporating leaven
Deeply modify a mass or group through the presence of a small element
Morally corrupt or contaminate
G2220.detail:
1. Leaven is a substance (yeast or leftover fermented dough) that is mixed with flour and water: it makes it rise and become light. Jesus uses this image in His parable of the kingdom: "a woman took and mixed [leaven] in three measures of flour, until the whole dough was leavened" (Matthew 13:33). The process is silent and gradual, like the kingdom of God that spreads from within.

2. The image extends to any discreet but powerful influence: "a little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6, Galatians 5:9). A small amount of leaven is enough to transform a large mass. Paul applies it to sin or malice in the assembly: a person who accepts evil "leavens" the whole community, infecting it as leaven permeates the dough.

3. The word thus carries the idea of moral contamination or corruption: the leaven of sin "leavens" the Christian community if it is not rejected. That is why Paul urges to purify the community (1 Corinthians 5:6-8).
G2220.origine: The verb comes from the noun leaven (zymē in Greek). The image goes back to the actual process of the ancient baker: mixing leaven into the dough transforms it from within. In Hebrew, the word chametz (leaven) evokes fermentation and effervescence. Leaven was forbidden at the Jewish Passover, symbolizing the absence of corruption. The Greek verb directly translates this physical reality before becoming a spiritual image.
G2220.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, only in Matthew and Luke (twice) and in Paul (twice). In Matthew and Luke (13:21, 13:33), it is the parable of the leaven: Jesus describes the kingdom of heaven as a small amount of leaven that leavens a whole dough — an image of silent and total growth. In Paul (1 Corinthians 5:6, Galatians 5:9), the meaning deepens: leaven becomes an image of pernicious influence or malice. The context in 1 Corinthians 5 shows that it concerns the impact of sin in the church if tolerated. The image remains the same (a little is enough to transform everything), but Paul directs it towards warning rather than hope.
G2220.portee: This word teaches the Christian two lessons: first, that the kingdom of God acts silently, from within, without noise, gradually transforming everything like leaven leavens the dough — a comfort for those who doubt the effectiveness of God's reign. Second, it warns that the influence of evil, no matter how small, corrupts the community: spiritual vigilance and purification are essential. The word reminds us that nothing we tolerate in faith remains without effect.

sens: To catch a living animal or person, to take them prisoner
In a figurative sense, to exert control over someone, to seize them
To conquer or attract someone to a cause, especially spiritual
G2221.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: to capture a living animal or person, without killing them. It is a word of hunting and warfare. In Luke 5:10, Jesus plays on this meaning by telling Simon Peter that he will now be a fisher of men — the image is that of a net catching fish alive to bring them back, transposed to the apostolic mission.
2. The word can also express a takeover, a domination. In 2 Timothy 2:26, Paul says that the devil has taken people captive (in the passive) — he holds them captive in his traps, controls them, submits them to his will.
3. By extension, the word can evoke the irresistible attraction that draws someone into a project or allegiance: to capture someone to make them one’s own, to engage them in a cause.
G2221.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "living" (ζωός, zôos) and "to hunt, to catch" (ἀγρεύω, agreuô). Its underlying image is that of the hunter or fisherman who captures his prey alive, intact. The underlying Hebrew word in the Greek Old Testament is often a form of the verb חיה (hiw), which means "to live." It is a word specifically formed to mean "to capture alive," which implies an intention: one does not want to kill, but to take.
G2221.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 5:10, Jesus uses it to describe the mission of the apostles: they will be "fishers of men," capturing living men to bring them to Him. The image is that of a miraculous catch transformed into a spiritual mission. In 2 Timothy 2:26, Paul uses it in the passive: the men deceived by the devil are "captured" by him, caught in his traps, held under his control until they regain their senses and escape. The word emphasizes everywhere the idea of living capture and control, never destruction.
G2221.portee: This word reveals two contradictory calls: on one side, Jesus captures men for life, freedom, and salvation (Luke 5:10); on the other, the devil captures them for enslavement and perdition (2 Timothy 2:26). The Christian must understand that there is a struggle for the soul at stake, and that only Christ offers a capture — a call — that truly liberates. The word also invites each disciple not to remain passive: being a "fisher of men" means seeking to draw others to Christ with gentleness and life, not with force or threat.

sens: physical and biological existence, as the duration of vital breath
the life of the person raised or restored to life after death
new existence, spiritual and moral life under the grace of God
eternal life, the promised glory of happiness for believers
that which gives life, the source of life
continuation of existence, prolongation of life
G2222.detail:
1. Natural life, the duration of our existence on earth, the act of breathing and existing day by day. Jesus tells his disciples: "Whoever loses their life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 16:25), meaning that giving up personal interests is not a loss.

2. The life of one who is brought back from the dead, or new existence after death. Jesus declares: "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25), affirming that he has the power to give new life to those who are dead.

3. The way of living according to God, in communion with Him through grace. The Apostle Paul says: "You have your fruit to holiness, and the end everlasting life" (Romans 6:22), signifying a transformed existence that depends on obedience to God.

4. Endless life, the fullness of happiness beyond time. John states: "God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son" (1 John 5:11), designating the blessed destiny reserved for believers.

5. Christ himself, or that which proceeds from Him, considered as the source of spiritual life. Paul writes: "Christ, who is your life, will appear" (Colossians 3:4), emphasizing that all true life depends on His action.

6. The perpetuation of existence, the act of continuing to live. When Jesus speaks of "the narrow way that leads to life" (Matthew 7:14), he refers to the path that leads to salvation and blessed continuation.
G2222.origine: The Greek word zōē comes from an ancient root meaning "living" or "to live." In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew word hayîm ("life" or "the living"). Greek distinguishes zōē (life as existence and vital energy) from bíos (the manner of living, the kind of life). In the Bible, zōē progressively emphasizes life as a gift from God and communion with Him, far beyond the mere physiological act of breathing.
G2222.emploi: The word appears 128 times in the New Testament, with a remarkable concentration in John (more than one-third of the occurrences). In John, zōē carries a profound theological significance: it is the life that God offers through His Son (John 6:51, 53), a life that begins now through faith and continues eternally (John 4:14). Mark and Luke speak of eternal life in connection with the inheritance of the kingdom of God (Mark 10:30, Luke 18:30). Paul distinguishes between carnal life and spiritual life: it is an existence governed by the Spirit, freed from sin, leading to salvation (Romans 6:22, 8:6). In Matthew, "life" is the treasure found by following Jesus on the narrow path (Matthew 7:14, 19:16-17). The word thus encompasses physical existence but culminates in the revelation of eternal and spiritual life.
G2222.portee: For the believer, understanding this word illuminates a central promise of the Gospel: authentic life is not about accumulating years or wealth, but entering into a living relationship with God through Christ. Jesus announces that this life begins here and now for those who believe, and it will never cease. It is an invitation to reevaluate what we mean by "truly living": not earthly survival, but communion with God and walking according to His Spirit.

sens: A strip of fabric or leather that surrounds the waist or chest
A symbolic object of dignity, power, or sacredness
Pocket or receptacle for carrying money
G2223.detail:
1. It is primarily a practical garment: a strip tied around the body to hold clothing in place or to gird the loins for action. John the Baptist wears a leather belt (Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6), which characterizes his austerity.
2. In glorious or solemn scenes, the belt takes on symbolic value: it signifies dignity and power. The Son of Man in John's vision wears a golden belt around his chest (Revelation 1:13), an image of royalty and sacredness; the angels in Revelation are girded with golden belts, a sign of their heavenly status.
3. The belt also serves as a purse or pouch: money and small objects are slipped into it. Jesus instructs his disciples not to take gold or silver in their belts when he sends them on mission (Matthew 10:9 and Mark 6:8), as they must trust in God alone.
G2223.origine: The Greek word ζώνη comes from the verb ζώννυμι which means "to gird, to surround." It generally translates, in the Greek version of the Old Testament, the Hebrew words אַבְנֵט (abnet, priest's belt) and חֲגוֹר (hagor, belt in general). It is a concrete word that depicts an everyday object, but it has early acquired symbolic resonances, especially in theophany narratives where celestial beings or the divine appear girded with sumptuous belts.
G2223.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, always to designate this specific object. In the Synoptics, it primarily refers to the belt of John the Baptist, ascetic and prophet (Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6), and then to Jesus' advice to his apostles to be without it during their proclamation mission (Matthew 10:9 and Mark 6:8)—this absence being a sign of detachment and trust. In Acts 21:11, the belt becomes a prophetic gesture: Agabus girds himself with Paul's belt to symbolically signify his capture in Jerusalem. In Revelation (1:13 and 15:6), it takes on a celestial and royal splendor, of gold, a sign of the glory and power of the Son of Man and His angels.
G2223.portee: This belt reminds us that material detachment is a trait of the authentic disciple—Jesus invites His apostles to freedom of movement and dependence on the Father rather than accumulation. Conversely, seeing Christ clothed in a golden belt in John's vision reinforces the assurance that He who reigns over the Church is clothed in glory and power; it is a reason for confidence when facing trials.

sens: To tighten something around the waist or body with a belt or band
To dress, to equip oneself by putting on clothes and accessories
To prepare or arrange someone for an action
G2224.detail:
1. Gird literally means to wrap a belt or band around the waist. In John 21:18, Jesus tells Peter that when he was young, he girded himself — he fastened his belt to be ready to move freely. It is a practical and daily gesture to keep one's clothing in place.
2. The word also describes the action of dressing, preparing by putting on or adjusting one's clothes. In Acts 12:8, the angel commands the imprisoned Peter: "Gird your belt and sandals," meaning equip yourself and prepare to leave. It is a call to dress completely.
3. Figuratively, gird evokes physical and moral preparation to accomplish a task or endure a trial. In ancient times, girding was preparing for action, labor, or suffering — which is why Jesus says that Peter, when old, would no longer have the strength to gird himself to go where he wished.
G2224.origine: The verb ζώννυμι comes from the Greek noun ζώνη (zônê), which literally means belt or zone. The root evokes the idea of surrounding or girding. In Hebrew, the same imagery is found with the verb חָגַר (hâgar), which also means to gird or to be girded. This imagery of girding is common in the ancient world: girding one's loins was primarily a practical gesture, then a posture of readiness and strength.
G2224.emploi: The verb gird appears only twice in the New Testament in French. The first occurrence (John 21:18) is in the past: Peter girded himself when he was young — an image of his active youth. The same phrase, in the future, describes him girded by another when he is old — a symbolic foreshadowing of his martyrdom, where he will no longer control his fate. The second occurrence (Acts 12:8) uses the related noun "belt" and the verb in the middle voice, for the practical order to equip oneself before fleeing. In both cases, the word oscillates between the concrete (dressing, preparing) and the symbolic (preparing a destiny, accepting a fate).
G2224.portee: For the Christian, girding is a biblical image of preparation and submission. To gird oneself expresses the autonomy and vigor of youth; to be girded by another expresses acceptance of trial and death. This passage from John 21 invites meditation on the transformation of our lives: from personal control to surrender into God's hands. It is a sober yet profound word about aging and grace in suffering.

sens: To keep someone alive, to make them survive
To preserve or save someone's life
To regain life, to come back to life
G2225.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to keep someone alive, to prevent them from dying. In Acts 7:19, the king of Egypt "exposed the children so that they would not live": he wants to kill them, while one who would preserve them alive would let them grow. It is the act of preserving physical existence.

2. Figuratively, "to preserve life" means to save one's life, to keep it for oneself instead of losing it. In Luke 17:33, Jesus says: "Whoever seeks to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will find it." Here the verb marks the anxious desire to preserve one's own existence.

3. The verb can also mean "to come back to life" or "to live" in an active sense. In 1 Timothy 6:13, it speaks of God "who gives life to all things": He is the one who maintains everything in existence and vitality.
G2225.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: zōos (living, alive) and gonē or goneía (to generate, to produce). Originally, it meant "to engender alive," that is, to give birth to a living being rather than a dead one. Over time, the meaning expanded to "to preserve alive," that is, to maintain what is living. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew hayah (to live) and forms of the verb "to vivify" (chiyah, hiphil of the root "to live").
G2225.emploi: This verb appears three times in the New Testament. In Luke 17:33, it is Jesus who uses it to express the spiritual paradox: wanting to save one's life by one's own efforts is to lose it; only he who abandons it for Christ truly preserves it. In Acts 7:19, it describes Pharaoh's intention to kill the Hebrew newborns, thus not allowing them to live. In 1 Timothy 6:13, Paul uses it to glorify God as the one who "gives life to all things" and who maintains the universe in existence. In each case, the verb speaks of the continuity of life — whether physically, spiritually, or in God's creative work.
G2225.portee: This word helps the reader understand the heart of the Gospel: true life is not gained by our efforts of preservation or self-protection. Jesus invites us to abandon anxious control to receive life from Him. For the Christian, this means that true life — lasting and eternal — comes not from clinging to our earthly concerns, but from losing ourselves in Christ. It is also a reminder that all life, from beginning to end, is a gift from God.

sens: An animal, a being endowed with life
G2226.detail: 1. The word designates a living being, animal or creature, characterized by the life that animates it. It is the most general term for speaking of everything that lives and moves. In Hebrews 13:11, it qualifies the sacrificed animals: "The bodies of the animals, whose blood is brought into the sanctuary..."
G2226.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "zōo-" (ζωο-) which means "life." It is in the same family as "zōé" (life) and "zōos" (living, animated). In Greek, this term expresses the idea of vital breath, of the being that breathes and lives. It often translates in Greek the Hebrew "chaï" (חַי, living), which designates everything that possesses life and animation.
G2226.emploi: The word appears about 20 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Revelation. It first designates ordinary terrestrial animals (Hebrews 13:11: the sacrificial animals; 2 Peter 2:12 and Jude 1:10: the irrational animals). But its main and striking usage concerns the four living creatures of Revelation, which surround the divine throne (Revelation 4:6-9, 5:6-14, 6:1-7, etc.). These "living creatures" are filled with eyes and participate in the liturgy of heaven, praising and worshiping God. The word emphasizes their created and animated nature, in contrast with the eternal God. It is a neutral and respectful term, never pejorative.
G2226.portee: This word reminds us that every living creature belongs to the created order and depends on God for its life. In Revelation, these celestial creatures show us that the worship of the Creator is at the heart of all created existence, from the humblest animal to the highest spiritual beings. Recognizing each living creature as dependent on God invites the believer to humility and reverence towards the Lord of all life.

sens: To give life, to make live, to animate
To resurrect, to bring back to life
To give spiritual life, to save
To make effective, to give power
G2227.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to give life or make live: it is the action of creating or communicating life to something. This is why God the Father "gives life" to the dead (Romans 4:17), and the Son gives life to whom he wills (John 5:21).
2. It also means to resurrect or bring back to life: in 1 Corinthians 15:22, Paul speaks of those who "will come to life in Christ," meaning that Christ will bring them back to life after death, just as he himself was resurrected.
3. For a Christian, this word also denotes spiritual life, the animation of the soul by the Spirit: "It is the Spirit who gives life," says Jesus in John 6:63, showing that it is the divine Spirit that gives true life, not the flesh.
4. It can finally mean to make effective or to give power: in 2 Corinthians 3:6, the Spirit "gives life," while the letter kills, for only the Spirit gives a transforming effectiveness to the Word.
G2227.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "living, life" (zoon in Greek) combined with an element that means "to make." It is a compound verb: "to make live." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb meaning "to give life" or "to keep alive." The word expresses the creative or restorative action that communicates life to one who does not have it or has lost it.
G2227.emploi: This verb appears 10 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in the Pauline epistles and in the Gospel of John. John uses it for both spiritual and physical resurrection: the Father resurrects the dead and gives life, and the Son does the same (John 5:21, 6:63). Paul sees it as both the future resurrection of believers (1 Corinthians 15:22, 1 Peter 3:18) and the present animation by the Spirit (Romans 8:11, 2 Corinthians 3:6, Galatians 3:21). The word thus designates both eschatological resurrection and the present spiritual life given by the Spirit.
G2227.portee: This word reveals that true life — the life worth living — comes from God alone, and that only the Spirit of Christ can give it. It reminds the Christian that their faith is not a human effort, but a divine animation that begins now and culminates in resurrection. It is a word of hope: where there is spiritual or physical death, God has the power to give life.

sens: Indicates an alternative between two or more possibilities
Introduces a question to ask which of two terms is true
Introduces an objection or correction to what has been said
Serves as a comparative: "more than," "less than"
Introduces a clarification: "that is to say" or "in other words"
Combines with other words to nuance the meaning
G2228.detail:
1. The most common meaning: to present two or more distinct choices. Between two simple words: "bread or water" (Luke 14:5: "his son or his ox"). Between complete ideas: "do this or that" (1 Corinthians 5:10: "with the immoral or with the greedy or with the idolaters").
2. In a question, to ask which of two things is true or possible. Jesus poses a diagnostic question: "Which is easier, to say to the paralytic: Your sins are forgiven, or to say: Get up?" (Mark 2:9). Often in debates with opponents: "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?" (Luke 6:9).
3. When refusing or contradicting what has just been said, introducing a correction or refutation: "Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, who would at once send me more than twelve legions of angels?" (Matthew 26:53) — here "or" marks the transition from the present to a possible future, an alternative.
4. After a comparative adjective or the verb "to want": expresses comparison. "There are higher or lower places" (Matthew 23:6 implicit). Jesus: "I would rather speak five words with my understanding than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue" (1 Corinthians 14:19) — here "or" conveys the comparative relationship.
5. Before an expression that explains or clarifies: "before they had lived together" = "before they were" (Matthew 1:18). Sometimes it equates to "that is to say."
6. In combination with other particles: "ἤ ... ἤ" ("either ... or"), "ἀλλ᾽ ἤ" ("but"), "ἤ καί" ("or even," "or also"). Galatians 1:8: "if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed" — the two "or" mark an accumulation of equally impossible alternatives.
G2228.origine: A very ancient word in Greek, it originally marked a separation between two things (its image is that of division, of choice). It can serve as a disjunctive conjunction ("or") or comparative ("than"). In the translation of the Greek Old Testament, it often renders the Hebrew אוֹ (ô), which has exactly the same function. Its history goes back to Indo-European; it is a fundamental word in classical Greek and the New Testament, where it occurs in about 290 instances.
G2228.emploi: The conjunction "or" is extremely frequent in the New Testament (more than 280 times according to the Segond). It appears in all books, particularly in the words of Jesus, questions, and debates. Between two nouns: "bread or fish" (Luke 11:11). Between two verbs: "to praise or to blame" (Matthew 5:16 implicit). In diagnostic or objection questions: Jesus or his opponents pose an alternative to clarify thought (Mark 12:14: "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?"). It can also serve to reinforce a negation: "neither living nor dead" is expressed as "or living or dead." Rarely, it takes on a comparative nuance ("more than") after adjectives or certain verbs (Matthew 10:15).
G2228.portee: This small conjunction reflects the pedagogical clarity of Jesus: he poses questions that force a choice, that cut between good and evil, between the fear of man and obedience to God. It invites the reader not to remain neutral, to weigh the consequences of each proposed path. In reading the enumerative "or," one also discovers true priorities: "No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to one and despise the other" (Matthew 6:24) — no compromise is possible.

sens: to lead and administer a region or territory as a political leader
to exercise the authority of a governor
to command in chief during a military campaign
G2230.detail:
1. The primary and most general meaning of the word is "to lead" or "to be at the head of," particularly in a context of political authority. It conveys the idea of guiding, managing the affairs of a place or a people. In Luke 3:1, we see Pontius Pilate who "governs" Judea: he is the main responsible party, the one who exercises power.

2. More specifically, the word designates the function of a governor, that is, an administrator of a province. Luke 2:2 speaks of Quirinius who "was governor of Syria": he exercised Roman authority over this region. It is an official position, a post of political power.

3. The word can also evoke military command, the authority of one who leads an army in campaign. Although this meaning is less explicit in the two passages of the New Testament, it remains embedded in the root of the word and its history.
G2230.origine: The word comes from the root ἡγεμών (hēgemṓn), which means "one who leads," "one who directs," or "one who commands." It is a title of dignity among the Greeks and Romans. The verb is naturally derived from it: it is the action of doing what a governor does, exercising his role. The root itself comes from the verb that means "to lead forward."
G2230.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Luke and in a very specific historical context. In Luke 2:2 and 3:1, Luke uses it to chronologically and politically situate the events he reports: the birth of Jesus and the beginning of John the Baptist's ministry. In both cases, the verb designates the official position of Roman governor. Luke uses this word to remind us that these moments in the history of salvation occurred under a precise Roman administration, in a defined geography and authority. It reflects a concern of a faithful historian.
G2230.portee: This word reminds us that the life of Jesus took place in real history, under governors and earthly authorities. Luke thus situates us: the decisive events of salvation did not occur in the abstract or the myth, but in a concrete, measurable time and place, under the scrutiny of history. This reinforces the reliability of the Gospel narrative.

sens: Sovereign authority of a leader or a state
Period during which this authority is exercised
G2231.detail:
1. Sovereign authority of a leader or a state — This is the supreme power exercised by a sovereign or a king who commands a people or a territory. The image is that of government: someone who reigns, who decides, who controls. In Luke 3:1, "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar" refers to the political and military power that the emperor exercises over the Roman Empire.
2. Period during which this authority is exercised — The word can also refer to the duration, the span of time during which this sovereignty is exercised. Luke 3:1 illustrates this: an event (the beginning of John the Baptist's ministry) is measured in relation to a year of reign, that is, a year of the period during which Tiberius governs.
G2231.origine: The word comes from the root ἡγε- ("to lead," "to direct"), which also gives ἡγεμών ("chief," "sovereign," "governor"). Hēgemonia literally means "the action or state of one who leads," hence "government" or "reign." The Greek word translated in Luke 3:1 conveys a political concept of sovereignty and absolute authority, characteristic of Roman imperial power.
G2231.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament (Luke 3:1). In this historical and political context, Luke places it at the moment he sets the chronological and geographical framework of his narrative: he dates the baptism of Jesus according to the Roman calendar of Tiberius's power. This choice emphasizes the political authority that surrounded Israel at the time, while John the Baptist appears as a voice of God outside these power structures.
G2231.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus came to announce a kingdom that transcends earthly kingdoms, even that of Rome. It invites the reader to situate the story of Redemption within the real political history of this world, and to understand that true reign belongs to God, not to the powerful of the earth.

sens: Military or political leader who exercises command authority
Roman officer in charge of a province or territory
Roman magistrate who administers a region and dispenses justice
G2232.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a leader or guide who holds the authority to command. It is someone who exercises the power of direction over a group or territory, like a military chief (Matthew 10:18).
2. More specifically, it refers to a high-ranking Roman officer sent to govern a province. This can include a proconsul, a propraetor, or a legate — different titles, but all designating Roman officials (Luke 21:12).
3. In the Gospels, the word mainly applies to the Roman procurator of Judea, such as Pontius Pilate, who dispenses justice and administers the region on behalf of Rome. Jesus appeared before this governor (Matthew 27:11), who had the power to judge and condemn.
G2232.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to lead, to conduct, to guide." It designates one who leads — a leader or chief. In ancient Hebrew, similar words were used to refer to tribal chiefs or princes. The Greek word translates several Hebrew terms designating leaders and authorities.
G2232.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. It regularly applies to the Roman governor of Judea — Pontius Pilate during the trial of Jesus (Matthew 27:2, 27:11, 27:21). It is also encountered in warnings of persecution: Jesus announces that his disciples will be brought before governors (Luke 21:12, Acts 23:33).
