G2273.detail: 1. In Romans 6:16, the word marks a logical disjunction: "either of sin which leads to death, or of obedience which leads to righteousness." It presents two exclusive options, without gradation: you serve one or the other of these two masters, period. It is the particle of a sharp alternative, which forces the reader to choose between two opposing paths.
G2273.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek ἤτοι (ètoi), composed of ἤ (or) and τοι (intensifying particle). In Homer, it meant "certainly, truly"; it later took on the meaning of "either... or" by presenting alternatives. It is an epic and solemn particle, rarely used in the New Testament.
G2273.emploi: This word appears only once in the entire New Testament, in Romans 6:16. Paul uses it in a pressing moral argument: he asks the Christians in Rome if they are unaware that by offering themselves as slaves to someone, they become slaves of that one. To clarify his thought, he uses this disjunctive particle, either to enumerate the two possible servitudes — servitude of sin or of obedience — or to emphasize that the choice of master is inevitable and without escape.
G2273.portee: This word reminds us of a decisive spiritual truth: every human being serves something or someone. There is no moral neutrality. The Bible forces the reader to recognize that they are a slave — either to sin which leads to death, or to obedience which leads to righteousness. This clear choice helps every Christian to measure the seriousness of their daily decisions: each of our allegiances brings us closer to one mastery or the other.

sens: To be inferior or disadvantaged compared to someone else
To be dominated, surpassed, or mastered by a force, a person, or a passion
G2274.detail:
1. The word describes a situation where one is treated less favorably than others. Paul asks the Corinthians how they have been "less favorably" treated compared to other churches, since he has not been a burden to them (2 Corinthians 12:13): there is here an inferiority of treatment.
2. The word primarily means to be defeated, dominated, mastered by something that surpasses us. In 2 Peter 2:19, those who promise freedom are in reality "slaves of what has triumphed over them": passion or vice has defeated them and holds them captive. This is the sense of a moral defeat.
G2274.origine: The word comes from a root expressing inferiority or weakness (related to ἥσσων, "less," "inferior"). Its basic image is that of being "less" in the sense of not measuring up against something stronger. This notion of inferiority naturally enriches towards the meaning of "being defeated" or "being dominated": one is inferior to the force that overwhelms them.
G2274.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in the passive voice: it describes a condition endured rather than an action undertaken. In 2 Corinthians 12:13, Paul uses it ironically to refer to a minor shortcoming in his ministry. In 2 Peter 2:19-20, it takes on a moral gravity: it depicts those seduced by false teachers as men defeated and enslaved by their own passions. The context emphasizes that the freedom promised by the corrupters is illusory, since these masters themselves are slaves of what has defeated them.
G2274.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that there is a moral reality to victory and defeat: one who allows themselves to be dominated by sin or by false doctrine is not free, but captive. It invites one not to be seduced by those who preach freedom while being themselves "defeated" internally. It is a call to spiritual vigilance and to seek true freedom in Christ alone.

sens: Decrease, reduction in quantity or value
Loss, what is lacking for completeness
Defect, shortcoming in what one should be
Defeat, setback in a struggle or trial
G2275.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a measurable decrease: in Romans 11:12, the "diminution" of the Jews (their temporary rejection of the Gospel) has paradoxically enriched the world by opening salvation to the Gentiles. It is a numerical or spiritual reduction.
2. More broadly, it refers to what is lacking, what is missing for something to be whole or accomplished. The defect creates a gap, an incompleteness.
3. The word can also signify a moral shortcoming or defect in the Christian life. In 1 Corinthians 6:7, having lawsuits among brothers is termed a "defect": it is a failure to meet the ideal of love and reconciliation that Christ demands.
4. In a context of struggle or trial, it expresses defeat or setback: a loss of position or victory.
G2275.origine: The word comes from the root ἥττη (hêttê), which means "inferiority" or "defeat." It is a regularly formed noun that designates the state of one who is defeated or diminished. The family of words around ἥττη always evokes some form of retreat, weakening, or loss. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), the word sometimes renders the Hebrew that expresses reduction or decline.
G2275.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament. The first occurrence, in Romans 11:12, is found in Paul's great reflection on the role of Israel in the history of salvation: the temporary "diminution" of the Jews has providentially served the extension of the Gospel to the Gentiles. The second, in 1 Corinthians 6:7, criticizes lawsuits among Christians as a "defect," a weakness and unfaithfulness to the message of grace. These two usages reveal how an apparent loss or shortcoming can become an occasion for redemption or a call to repentance.
G2275.portee: This word reminds the believer that setbacks and shortcomings are not outside of divine providence. In Romans, the temporary diminution of Israel fits into God's plan for the salvation of all. In 1 Corinthians, it invites us to recognize our defects — lawsuits, rivalries — and to seek reconciliation rather than worldly victory. It is an invitation to see beyond appearances.

sens: Weaker, inferior in quality or value
Worse, more bad
With less intensity, less abundantly
G2276.detail:
1. The word denotes what is inferior to something else. In Corinth, the gatherings become "worse" instead of better: what Paul reproaches is that their gathering does not elevate them but lowers them (1 Corinthians 11:17). It is a judgment on quality: something that worsens instead of improving.
2. Here, the meaning shifts towards "worse" or "more bad": assemblies that divide and hurt are morally worse than no assembly at all. It is a negative state, a degradation.
3. Applied to a feeling or relationship, the word can also mean "less" in a quantitative sense: Paul fears being "less" loved by the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 12:15) — not hated, but with less affection, less warmth. It is the intensity or abundance that diminishes.
G2276.origine: This Greek word comes from a root expressing the idea of weakness or inferiority. It belongs to a family of comparison: ἥσσων is situated between "good" and "bad," indicating always a movement downwards, a decrease in value or strength. In the Greek Bible, it often translates the Hebrew וַיִּשְׁמַר ("to be defeated" or "to succumb"), as the inferior is the one who loses against the stronger.
G2276.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Corinthians 11:17, Paul uses it to criticize how the Corinthians gather: instead of coming out stronger or more united, they become "worse." In 2 Corinthians 12:15, it takes on a nuance of quantity: Paul generously expends himself for the Corinthians, accepting the risk of being loved "less" in return. In both cases, the word expresses a degradation or loss — of good or of love.
G2276.portee: This word invites the believer to examine the real impact of their communal life. Do gatherings, assemblies, and fraternal relationships make us better or worse? Paul reminds us that the true church does not merely exist; it must build up, elevate, and sanctify. It is also a word of pastoral humility: the servant of God can give much and receive little in return. This does not deter them from their love.

sens: To produce a sound that propagates and reverberates
To ring out with force or clarity
To echo, to make noise
G2278.detail:
1. To resonate means to emit a sound that fills the space and reverberates. The image is that of a musical instrument or metal that vibrates and produces a loud noise: in 1 Corinthians 13:1, Paul speaks of a brass instrument that "resonates," meaning it emits a loud but hollow sound.
2. The word also evokes the idea of ringing out, of making intense noise: it is the sound that strikes the ear with force, like that of a cymbal in 1 Corinthians 13:1.
3. Figuratively, to resonate can mean to have an impact or to make noise around oneself. But for Paul, this noise without charity is nothing but empty sound.
G2278.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἦχος (échos), which means "noise," "sound." It is the root of our French word "écho." The verb ἠχέω adds the idea of action: to make noise, to produce a sound. In ancient translations of the Old Testament into Greek, this verb often renders Hebrew words expressing noise, rumbling, or tumult.
G2278.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 13:1. Paul uses it to describe the sound produced by brass or a cymbal: a loud and resounding noise, but which remains meaningless if not animated by charity. The usage is metaphorical: one who speaks in tongues or utters words without love for others is merely an instrument that resonates, that is, makes hollow noise.
G2278.portee: This word reminds us that beautiful speeches, even spectacular gifts of the Spirit, have value only if they spring from love. A noise that resonates without heart builds nothing. It is an invitation to seek substance before appearance, and love before the prestige of gifts.

sens: A physical sound, a vibration of air that can be heard
A powerful rumble or crash
A news that spreads, a reputation
G2279.detail:
1. Noise is primarily a sound that is perceived — any sound that can be heard. On the day of Pentecost, the disciples suddenly hear from heaven "a noise like that of a violent wind" (Acts 2:2): it is not the wind itself, but the sound it produces.
2. Sometimes, this noise is particularly intense or impressive, a real crash. Luke mentions "the noise of the sea and the waves" (Luke 21:25), these terrifying and chaotic sounds that accompany cataclysms. Sinai resonated with the "sound of the trumpet" (Hebrews 12:19), a powerful and solemn sound that terrified the people.
3. The word can also mean a rumor or a fame that spreads: "his fame spread" (Luke 4:37) — the noise that is talked about, the reputation that circulates about a person.
G2279.origine: The Greek word ἦχος (ēchos) is related to the idea of resonance and echo. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates הָמוֹן (hamôn), which means noise, tumult, or a noisy crowd — the idea of collective resonance. The word itself carries the image of a vibration that propagates: a sound that repeats, that travels, hence the extension to the meaning of rumor or news that circulates.
G2279.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament. Twice, it refers to a concrete physical sound: the wonderful noise of the wind at Pentecost (Acts 2:2) and the terrifying noises of cataclysms (Luke 21:25). Once, it evokes a majestic and impressive sound, the noise of the trumpet at Sinai (Hebrews 12:19). Lastly, it shifts towards the meaning of rumor or fame that spreads: the fame of Jesus (Luke 4:37). This last meaning shows that noise, in the sense of circulating words, can be the source of a reputation.
G2279.portee: This word reminds us that God also manifests Himself through what we hear. The noise of the wind at Pentecost symbolizes the arrival of the Holy Spirit: it is a tangible phenomenon that testifies to an invisible reality. It invites us to be attentive to the signs that God manifests through words, noise, concrete events — and not to reduce faith to abstractions. It is also a reminder that the fame of Jesus spreads audibly and visibly: it is not hidden, it resounds.

sens: one of the twelve apostles of Jesus
a disciple also called Lebbaeus or Jude
G2280.detail:
1. Thaddeus is one of the twelve men that Jesus chose to be His apostles, His closest companions. He appears in the lists of apostles in Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18, where he is named alongside Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, and other disciples.
2. This apostle is also known by other names: Lebbaeus ("man of heart") and Jude, son of James. These three names refer to the same person, which is common for disciples of that time.
G2280.origine: The name Thaddeus comes from Aramaic and probably means "breast" or "bosom," evoking the idea of generosity or strength. It is a typical name in the Jewish context where Jesus chose His apostles. The same man is called Lebbaeus in some manuscripts, showing how disciples sometimes had multiple names or nicknames.
G2280.emploi: Thaddeus is mentioned only twice in the Gospels: in the list of the twelve apostles in Matthew 10:3 and in Mark 3:18. These two passages enumerate the names of the disciples that Jesus called to follow Him and participate in His ministry. Unlike Peter, John, or Judas, Thaddeus does not intervene in any specific narrative in the Gospels: he remains a figure in the background, one of the twelve faithful companions of Jesus.
G2280.portee: Thaddeus reminds the believer that not all disciples of Jesus have the same visibility or well-known role. Many servants of God remain discreet, without great renown, yet they are part of the chosen companions of the Lord. It is an invitation to humility and faithfulness, even when one does not shine under the spotlight.

sens: Expanse of salt water: ocean, sea, gulf, or strait
Lake or large body of fresh water (like the Sea of Galilee)
The water of the sea as substance, surface, or depth
Whole of the created world (heaven, earth, sea)
Original chaos or hostile force to dominate
Innumerable multitude of people
G2281.detail:
1. The sea primarily refers to any large expanse of salt water: the Mediterranean (where Paul sailed in Acts 27), the Red Sea (crossed by Israel in 1 Corinthians 10:1-2), or the strait between islands. This is the most common and literal meaning of the word.

2. The Bible also uses "sea" for significant freshwater lakes, particularly the Sea of Galilee where Jesus calls the disciples and walks on the water (Matthew 4:18, Mark 6:49). The Hebrew word יָם means both "sea" and "lake."

3. By the sea, one also refers to the substance itself: the water that rises in a storm (Matthew 8:24), on which one miraculously walks (Mark 6:49), or that one crosses to navigate (Acts 27:30, 27:40).

4. In Acts 4:24, "heaven, earth, and sea" expresses the entire universe in all its creation: it is a biblical way of saying "everything that exists."

5. In Revelation (Revelation 13:1), the sea symbolizes chaos, a source of threats and hostile powers — it echoes the creation narratives where the sea represents the absence of order before God's intervention.

6. In Romans 9:27, "the number of the sons of Israel would be like the sand of the sea" evokes an innumerable, incalculable crowd: the image emphasizes vastness.
G2281.origine: The Greek word θάλασσα comes from an ancient root that evokes agitation and vastness. In Hebrew, יָם (yam) means both "sea" and "lake," and Greek thalassa translates it in most occurrences of the Greek Old Testament. The word belongs to the fundamental vocabulary of Mediterranean peoples, for whom the sea was both a trade route, a source of food, and a formidable threat. No common Greek word really approaches it: πέλαγος (pelagos) refers more to the vast open ocean.
G2281.emploi: The word sea appears more than 80 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and Revelation. The Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) mention it mainly in the context of Jesus' ministry around the Sea of Galilee: calls of disciples, calmed storms, miracles. John also uses this term for the same lake. Acts describes several sea crossings, notably Paul's journey to Rome. Revelation uses "sea" symbolically and prophetically: source of chaos (13:1), element of divine creation (4:6), and spectacle of the end times (8:8, 16:3). The meaning thus varies between concrete (the body of water seen) and symbolic (the forces of disorder or vastness).
G2281.portee: The sea in the Bible reveals the power and absolute authority of Jesus: it reveres and obeys him (Mark 4:39-41). For the Christian reader, the sea reminds that nothing can escape the Lord's control — neither natural forces nor hostile powers. At the same time, the sea embodies a certain human fragility: it engulfs, it overwhelms, it isolates. It invites faith and trust in the one who walks on the waters and governs all.

sens: Warm, keep warm
Nurture tenderly, raise like a mother
Cherish, pamper
Surround with kind attentions
G2282.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is physical: to warm someone or something, to hold it close to protect it from the cold. It is the image of a blanket, of warmth given.
2. From this arises the image of a mother who tenderly feeds her child. In 1 Thessalonians 2:7, Paul says that the apostles were toward the Thessalonians "like a nursing mother takes care of her children": it is a maternal care, consisting of protection and nourishment of the little one.
3. The word extends to the idea of cherishing someone, treating them with particular affection, pampering them. In Ephesians 5:29, each man "nourishes and takes care" of his own body as Christ does for the Church: it is a constant kindness toward the one we love.
4. In all cases, "take care" implies conscious attention, tender vigilance, a willingness to nourish or protect the one being cared for.
G2282.origine: The Greek word θάλπω comes from a root that first evokes physical warmth, warming. The central image is that of a body receiving warmth, then that of the gentle protection that accompanies this warmth. In ancient Hebrew, we find related roots that also express the idea of taking care, keeping close. The metaphor naturally shifts from physical warmth to warmth of heart, to parental affection.
G2282.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Ephesians 5:29, it describes how each husband should treat his own body as Christ treats the Church: with constant nourishment and care. In 1 Thessalonians 2:7, Paul uses it to describe the attitude of the apostles toward the new Christians, compared to that of a nurse toward her children — tender, protective, nurturing. In both cases, the word expresses a care that unites physical nourishment and spiritual affection, vigilance and tenderness.
G2282.portee: This word reminds the believer that true care is not a cold obligation, but an act filled with tenderness and kindness. For the husband, it invites him to treat his wife with the gentleness of a mother. For pastors and spiritual leaders, it reminds that one can only guide souls with a maternal heart, softness combined with solid nourishment. It is also an image of Christ's love: he surrounds us like a mother surrounds her child.

sens: wife of Judah in the genealogy of Jesus
G2283.detail: Tamar is the Canaanite woman whom Judah married for his son Onan (Genesis 38). After the death of the latter, according to custom, Judah should have given her another son to perpetuate his lineage, but he refused. Tamar, by cunning, obtained from Judah himself two sons, Perez and Zerah. It is through Perez that the lineage of David and that of Jesus himself descends, as shown in the Gospel of Matthew by listing the ancestors of Christ.
G2283.origine: The Hebrew name תָּמָר literally means "palm tree." It is a common name in Israel, and Tamar symbolizes fertility and strength. The text of Genesis 38 recounts how she defended her right to offspring with remarkable boldness.
G2283.emploi: Tamar appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:3, in the genealogy of Jesus. She is one of the four women mentioned in this genealogy (along with Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba), which is very rare and significant. Her inclusion emphasizes that God includes in his plan of salvation women of humble or socially compromised condition, and that he honors those who act boldly for justice.
G2283.portee: The presence of Tamar in the genealogy of Jesus reveals that God does not exclude those whose history is complicated or whose actions are unconventional. She reminds us that redemption comes through unexpected means and that God's faithfulness surpasses our hasty moral judgments. For the reader, it is an invitation to see in Jesus not the fruit of an unblemished genealogy, but of a holy history where God works through our weaknesses.

sens: to be struck with intense amazement, to lose one's senses in the face of the unexpected
to be filled with fear or apprehension
to be terrified or overwhelmed by fear
G2284.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the state of someone who is struck by surprise or astonishment so strong that they almost lose their composure. This is what the disciples experience in Mark 1:27: after seeing Jesus command the unclean spirits with authority, they are "seized with astonishment" and ask one another what is happening. The astonishment temporarily paralyzes them.
2. The word can also denote a fear mixed with distress, an apprehension that overwhelms the soul. In Mark 10:32, the disciples going up to Jerusalem with Jesus are "troubled": they sense that something serious, a threat, is coming, and they follow him with fear.
3. In its strongest sense, the word expresses terror, the dread that seizes the body and mind. Saul in Acts 9:6, after his encounter with the risen Lord, is "seized with fear" — it is a visceral fear, that of a man facing a divine reality that surpasses and crushes him.
G2284.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes shock, sudden upheaval. It is formed from the noun θάμβος (trouble, astonishment). In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew בָּעַת (to be afraid, to be terrified), particularly in passive forms. This kinship shows that biblical Greek borrows from the Hebrew tradition the idea of a physical and emotional reaction to the extraordinary or the divine.
G2284.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, only in Mark and in Acts. Mark uses it three times to describe the disciples' reaction to Jesus: in 1:27, in front of his authority over the spirits; in 10:24 and 10:32, mixed with other feelings (difficulty in believing, foreboding of the coming drama). In Acts 9:6, Saul is seized with fear by the vision of the risen Lord. The word thus carries several nuances: admiring astonishment, perplexing trouble, religious fear in the face of the divine. It always describes a strong and involuntary inner emotion.
G2284.portee: This word teaches the reader that the encounter with Jesus and with God profoundly shakes those who experience it. It is not a light or superficial feeling, but something that seizes the whole being. For the Christian, this invites us not to trivialize the presence and work of the Lord, and to recognize that true faith often begins with this kind of astonishment before the greatness of God.

sens: Sudden shock caused by an extraordinary or unexpected sight
Fear mixed with admiration in the face of the marvelous
State of immobility or silence caused by surprise
G2285.detail:
1. Astonishment is the emotional shock that paralyzes for a moment when one sees something extraordinary. In Luke 4:36, the crowd is seized with astonishment upon hearing Jesus command the unclean spirits with an authority never seen before: it is wonder in the face of the superhuman.
2. It is also respectful fear mixed with admiration in the face of a miracle. In Luke 5:9, Peter and his companions are seized with terror (the same word) because of the miraculous catch of fish: they have never experienced anything like it, and it deeply troubles them.
3. Astonishment can render one speechless or paralyzed: in Acts 3:10, the people recognize the beggar miraculously healed and are filled with amazement, as if struck with astonishment at what he has become.
G2285.origine: The Greek word thambos expresses the idea of mental striking, of shock. It describes the psychic state of one who receives an invisible blow of admiration or fear. This word belongs to the family of verbs that express seizing, striking, moving. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates Hebrew words like pachad (fear, fright) or nismah (agitation), to designate the affect that seizes someone in the face of the divine or the marvelous.
G2285.emploi: The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, all in the Gospels and Acts. In Luke 4:36, it is the astonishment of the crowd before Jesus' new authority in commanding demons. In Luke 5:9, it is the astonishment of Peter and his companions before the miracle of the catch. In Acts 3:10, it is the astonishment of the witnesses recognizing the former beggar healed. In all cases, astonishment is the immediate and involuntary reaction of the witness in the face of a manifestation of the divine that exceeds the ordinary: it is the admission of the spectator that he is witnessing the extraordinary.
G2285.portee: The astonishment described in these accounts shows how the work of God provokes in the witnesses not an intellectual understanding at first, but an emotional shock that makes them available. This initial emotion is often the beginning of faith: it recognizes that something is happening that escapes ordinary explanations. For the reader, the astonishment of the biblical witnesses validates the reality of the reported miracles and reminds us that the action of God should move and transform us, not only intellectually, but in our whole being.

sens: that causes or can cause death
that has the power to kill
that brings destruction, an end
G2286.detail:
1. The word describes something — here, a poison — capable of causing death. In Mark 16:18, Jesus promises his disciples that a deadly drink will not harm them: the adjective refers to a poisonous liquid, which would normally have the effect of killing whoever drinks it.
2. More broadly, it applies to anything that carries within it the power to destroy or annihilate life. It conveys the idea of a fatal threat, a danger that can be deadly.
G2286.origine: The word comes from the Greek root θάνατος (thanatos), which means "death." It is an adjective formed from the noun: θανάσιμος describes what belongs to death, what is close to it, what bears its mark. The same root also composes "euthanasia" in modern French ("good death").
G2286.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 16:18. Jesus lists the signs that will accompany those who believe in him: casting out demons, speaking in new tongues, picking up serpents, and drinking poison without dying, laying hands on the sick. In this context, "mortal" qualifies a poisoned drink, and its use emphasizes the extraordinary nature of the promise: what would kill an ordinary man will have no effect on the believer.
G2286.portee: This verse invites the believer to meditate on the power of God that can preserve those who trust in him, even in the face of seemingly inevitable threats of death. The word "mortal" emphasizes that this is not a simple benign illness, but a real danger, a true destructive power that God overcomes. It speaks to faith in a divine protection that transcends the natural course of things.

sens: That brings or carries death
Containing a poison or venom capable of killing
Extremely dangerous and harmful
G2287.detail:
1. The word literally designates that which brings death, that which kills — something truly fatal. It conveys the idea of a snake's poison or a weapon that strikes fatally.
2. It primarily applies to that which contains a deadly poison: the venom of a venomous beast, the venom of a word that wounds mortally. James uses it for the tongue: it is "full of deadly poison" (James 3:8), meaning it contains within it a power of destruction like the venom of a serpent.
3. Figuratively, the word qualifies that which is extremely dangerous and harmful to spiritual and moral life: a word, an influence that ravages the soul as death ravages the body.
G2287.origine: The Greek word is composed of "thanatos" (death) and "pherô" (to carry, to bring). Literally: "that carries death." It is a natural image to qualify that which kills, that which is fatal. The composition suggests an active force, something that transports or communicates death, like a spreading venom.
G2287.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 3:8. The apostle James speaks of the tongue as an uncontrollable member, full of deadly poison. This venom represents the destructive power of wicked words, lies, curses: they kill as poison kills. The image of deadly venom emphasizes the urgency and seriousness of the problem — the tongue is not just "a small sin"; it is a deadly weapon that one carries within.
G2287.portee: This word reminds the Christian that words are never neutral. Words can spiritually and morally kill, deeply wound, destroy souls. James warns us: we are responsible for what we say. This invites vigilance and prayer, so that our tongue may be healed and become a source of life, not death.

sens: Cessation of biological life of the human body
Condemnation to be executed
Peril or deadly situation
Spiritual death: separation from God due to sin
Eternal death: final judgment and separation from God
G2288.detail:
1. The death of the body, natural or violent: it is the cessation of physical life. The Bible speaks of it directly, as when it reports that Jesus spoke of his own death (John 11:13) or that Enoch "did not see death" as God took him alive (Hebrews 11:5). The word opposes life: it is the fate of every man.

2. Legal condemnation to capital punishment: when judges declare that a person has "deserved death" (Acts 26:31, Luke 23:15). It is death pronounced as judicial punishment.

3. A danger, a deadly peril: "the region and shadow of death" (Matthew 4:16) refers to the spiritual darkness where men are in extreme peril, not even knowing they are dying.

4. Spiritual death caused by sin: sin produces moral and inner death (Romans 7:13), separating the soul from God. Those who do not listen to the word of Christ remain in this state (John 5:24).

5. The definitive death of divine judgment: the second judgment, hell, from which no one returns (Revelation 2:11). It is the eternal separation from God, more terrible than the death of the body.
G2288.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to die." In Hebrew and Aramaic, it translates the word "mout," which evokes both natural death and annihilation. The Greek Old Testament also uses it for certain words meaning "destruction" or "plague." It is a fundamental word that touches the universal experience: death is the fate of all men (Romans 5:12).
G2288.emploi: The word "death" appears more than 100 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and Revelation. It primarily denotes physical death: that of Christ, that of all men, and the deadly perils faced by the apostles (2 Corinthians 11:23). But Paul gives the word a theological depth: he speaks of the spiritual death that sin brings (Romans 7:13), of the "wages" of sin which is death (Romans 6:23), and of the liberation that Christ brings (2 Corinthians 4:12). John also emphasizes the passage from death to life through faith (John 5:24). Finally, Revelation speaks of the "second death," the final judgment (Revelation 2:11; 21:8). Thus, death is both a biological reality, a moral penalty, and an eternal issue.
G2288.portee: Death, in Scripture, is not a simple transition: it is the wages of sin and the absolute limit of man. But the New Testament always considers it in the light of Christ: his death for us (Romans 5:10) breaks the power of death and opens the way to resurrection. The Christian can therefore face death, knowing that Christ has conquered it. It is a call not to live in the spiritual death of sin, but to pass from death to life through faith.

sens: To kill someone, to take their life
To condemn to death, to decree someone's death
To mortify, to render powerless (figurative sense)
G2289.detail:
1. To put to death means to take someone's life, to kill them. This is the literal sense of the word. In the Gospels, the religious authorities seek to put Jesus to death: "The chief priests and all the council sought testimony against Jesus, to put him to death" (Mark 14:55). It is a violent and deliberate act.
2. To condemn to death is to pronounce or decree someone's death by an official sentence. The context of trials shows the judicial sense: one does not kill on the spot, but first judges to condemn. Thus, children who rise against their parents "will put them to death" (Matthew 10:21) suggests an act of authority or a fatal power grab.
3. Figuratively, to put to death means to mortify, weaken, or annihilate a power within us. Paul writes: "If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13). Here, it is to put to death sin and carnal desires, not to take physical life.
G2289.origine: The Greek word comes from "thanatos" (death, demise) to which a verbal suffix meaning "to cause" or "to make" is added. It literally means "to cause death," "to render mortal." In Hebrew, the verbs "to die" (with intensive forms) or "to kill" are rendered by this word in texts translated into ancient Greek. The family includes the noun "thanatos" and the adjective "thanatēs" (mortal).
G2289.emploi: This verb appears 11 times in the New Testament. It is very frequent in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) to describe the plots against Jesus or the persecutions of the disciples: the authorities seek him to put him to death. Paul uses it in his letters with a deeper and spiritual meaning: in Romans 8:13, he speaks of putting to death the works of the body by the Spirit (an action of holiness), and in Romans 7:4, he refers to being put to death to the law by the body of Christ (a spiritual rupture). The meaning thus varies between physical murder or condemnation and the annihilation or rupture of a spiritual power.
G2289.portee: This word helps the reader understand the gravity of the threats against Jesus and his disciples: it was not an abstract opposition, but a real murderous plot. For the Christian, the figurative use in Romans 8:13 reminds him of his spiritual responsibility: living fully for Christ requires "mortifying" — that is, silencing and weakening — the sinful desires that animate our flesh. It is a call to holiness, not by our own strength, but by the Spirit.

sens: To place a corpse in a tomb or grave
To pay final respects to a deceased person through a funeral ceremony
Figuratively: to abandon, to leave behind
G2290.detail:
1. To bury means to properly place a body in a tomb or grave. It is the physical act of interment. In Luke 16:22, the rich man "was buried" refers to the completion of these funeral rites; in Acts 5:6, Ananias is "buried" after his death.
2. The word also denotes the entire funeral rite that honors the deceased: washing the body, wrapping it in a shroud, speaking words, accompanying it to the grave. It is a familial and religious duty: in Matthew 8:21 and Luke 9:59, the disciple asks Jesus to "first go and bury my father," an expected act of filial piety.
3. Figuratively, Jesus uses "to bury" to mean "to abandon" or "to let go": in Matthew 8:22 and Luke 9:60, "let the dead bury their own dead" means that those who do not follow Him, who refuse His call, are already spiritually dead, and the disciple must leave them to their fate to follow Him.
G2290.origine: The Greek word θάπτω comes from a root that evokes the action of placing in the ground, of covering. In the Greek Old Testament, it regularly translates the Hebrew קָבַר (qabar), which has the same concrete meaning: to place a body in a tomb. This image of burial in the earth is at the heart of the word, reminding that death returns the body to dust.
G2290.emploi: The verb "to bury" appears 11 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew and Luke. It appears in three main contexts: first, the requests of disciples to Jesus (Matthew 8:21, Luke 9:59) to fulfill the funeral duty towards their fathers; second, the narration of the funerals of John the Baptist (Matthew 14:12) and Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:6, 9-10, 2:29); finally, the burial of Christ (1 Corinthians 15:4), a key moment in the Easter narrative. Jesus turns the word figuratively to speak of spiritual death.
G2290.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the final honors paid to the dead are legitimate and honorable—a significant part of familial piety. But it also teaches, through the words of Jesus, that following Christ requires renouncing everything, even traditional obligations, and giving God absolute priority. The burial of Christ is ultimately the promise of His resurrection: He did not remain in the tomb.

sens: Father of Abraham in the genealogy of Christ
G2291.detail: Terah is the father of Abraham, mentioned in the genealogy that Luke traces back to Adam to show that Jesus is the heir of all the promises of God made to Abraham's descendants. The text of Luke 3:34 presents him as the link in this genealogical chain: "son of Terah, son of Nahor," establishing the continuity of the lineage through which God has guided the history of salvation.
G2291.origine: The name Terah comes from the Hebrew תֶּרַח (Térakh), which literally means "breath" or "air," a poetic image of life. This name belongs to the patriarchal family: Terah is the son of Nahor and the father of Abraham, Nahor, and Haran, the latter being the father of Lot. The meaning of the name evokes the fragility and transience of human life, in the context of these ancient genealogies.
G2291.emploi: Terah appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:34, in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke. This evangelist traces the lineage of Jesus back to Adam through Abraham, and Terah appears as the immediate ancestor of Abraham. This place in the genealogy emphasizes that Jesus does not descend only from Abraham, but from a long chain of generations that God has sustained since the creation of the world. It is a reminder of the divine continuity in the history of salvation.
G2291.portee: Terah appears in the genealogy of Christ to remind that Jesus is part of a long history of humanity guided by God. His mention helps the reader see that the coming of the Messiah is not an accident or a surprise, but the culmination of a divine plan extending over generations. This reinforces the certainty that God's promises are reliable and that they are fulfilled according to His timetable.

sens: A feeling of security and inner assurance in the face of a situation
Moral courage that drives one to act or speak without fear
Certainty that one can rely on someone or something
G2292.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses an inner state of serenity and certainty: the one who has confidence does not doubt; they feel secure. Paul says in 2 Corinthians 5:6 that he is "full of confidence" knowing that even when away from the Lord, he remains under His protection. It is a peace that comes from the conviction of being on the right side.

2. Confidence becomes courage when it manifests in words or actions. In 2 Corinthians 10:1, Paul speaks of his "boldness" towards the Corinthians when he is away from them: he has the courage of his convictions and is not afraid to confront them if necessary. It is confidence that transforms into moral firmness.

3. Confidence also implies a relationship: one trusts someone because they believe them worthy of that trust. Paul says in 2 Corinthians 7:16: "I rejoice that I can be confident in you in all things"—he relies on them, he believes in their faithfulness. In Hebrews 13:6, it is the believer's confidence in the Lord that allows them to say: "I will not fear; what can man do to me?"
G2292.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek family related to the idea of courage and warmth (the Greek θάρσος means "courage"). It is a later form gradually replacing θαρσέω. The verb reflects a disposition of the soul: the one who has confidence feels "warm," energetic, ready to act without hesitation. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates contexts where God calls His people not to fear and to advance with assurance.
G2292.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, concentrated in Paul’s writings, particularly in his letters to the Corinthians. In 2 Corinthians 5:6 and 5:8, confidence is that of the Christian in the face of death and eternity: knowing that they will be with the Lord reassures. In 2 Corinthians 7:16, Paul expresses his confidence in the community. In 2 Corinthians 10:1-2, the word describes the apostle's firmness in the face of those who despise him: he has the confidence of one who knows his divine mandate. Finally, in Hebrews 13:6, confidence in God is the foundation of the absence of fear. The verb thus emphasizes an inner conviction, peaceful but also courageous, that arises from the relationship with the Lord or with those in whom one believes.
G2292.portee: For the Christian, this word invites examination of the sources of their confidence. Is it based only on circumstances (wealth, health, human approval), or does it rest on God's promise? Paul teaches that true confidence frees from paralyzing doubt and the desire to please at all costs: it enables moral courage and frankness. It is a fruit of faith, transforming an anxious heart into a serene and firm heart.

sens: To be filled with confidence and moral strength in the face of fear or doubt
To regain confidence after being troubled or worried
To feel reassured and comforted by a word or presence
To face trials with assurance, relying on God
G2293.detail:
1. Taking courage means dispelling fear and moral weakness to be filled with confidence. This is the command Jesus gives to the paralytic in Matthew 9:2: "Take courage, my child," to reassure him before forgiving his sins. The word denotes an act of inner will: to regain oneself, to be spiritually strengthened.

2. It also means to regain one's assurance after being troubled or seized with fear. When the disciples see Jesus walking on the water, they are "troubled" and afraid; Jesus immediately tells them: "Take heart; it is I; do not be afraid" (Mark 6:50). Here, courage comes from recognizing His presence and power.

3. Finally, it is to feel comforted and reassured by a living word. The woman who touches Jesus' garment receives these words: "Take courage, daughter; your faith has healed you" (Matthew 9:22). This confidence is not a vague feeling: it rests on the action of God who is already at work.
G2293.origine: The word comes from a Greek root expressing confidence and the absence of fear. It appears mainly in the Gospels and Acts to convey calls to trust addressed by Jesus or the apostles to men and women who doubt or are afraid. It is a typically evangelical term: it captures the gesture of Jesus who gives strength and courage to those who encounter Him.
G2293.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, always in the imperative form (a command or call). The Gospels provide almost all the occurrences: Matthew (2:9 and 14:27), Mark (6:50 and 10:49), John (16:33), and Luke (8:48). Jesus alone uses this verb to speak to His disciples or to the sick whom He heals. In Matthew 9:2 and 9:22, He says "take courage" to those He heals, linking courage to faith and forgiveness. In Matthew 14:27 and Mark 6:50, He reassures the frightened disciples on the sea. In John 16:33, He calls the disciples to take courage in the face of the world's tribulations, reminding them that He has overcome the world. It is a word of comfort in the face of fear, doubt, or suffering.
G2293.portee: For the Christian, this word summarizes a fundamental call: in the face of fear, illness, or uncertainty, Jesus invites us to trust. Taking courage does not deny the difficult reality but faces it head-on while relying on the presence and power of God. It is an invitation to living faith, not to doubt or fear.

sens: Moral audacity, assurance in the face of danger or adversity
Confidence, strength of soul that drives to action
Source or foundation of confidence
Boldness, sometimes excessive or inappropriate
G2294.detail:
1. Courage is moral audacity, the strength of soul in the face of perils or obstacles. In Acts 28:15, when Paul sees the brothers coming to meet him, he "takes courage" — he regains his assurance and confidence in God amidst his trials. It is an inner disposition that restores vigor.
2. The word also denotes what gives courage, that is, the concrete reasons that ground confidence: seeing the brothers, feeling the support of the Church, receiving an encouraging word. It is the "why" of courage.
3. In a less positive sense, courage can turn into excessive boldness or misplaced audacity — self-confidence then becomes presumption or impudence. The context indicates whether it is a virtue or a flaw.
G2294.origine: The Greek word tharsos comes from an ancient root meaning "to have boldness" or "vigor." It is close to the word tharrheô (to dare, to be bold) and belongs to the family of θρασύς (audacious). In Hebrew, the corresponding word often translated is "leb" (heart) or "az" (strength), which express an inner strength of the soul.
G2294.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:15. Paul, after his long tribulations (shipwreck, captivity), meets the Christian brothers who come to seek him in Rome. At this sight, his heart revives: he "takes courage." It is a key moment where brotherly communion rekindles his confidence in God. The rarity of the word shows that it is a decisive moment in the narrative of Acts.
G2294.portee: This passage invites the Christian to understand that true courage does not come from our own strength, but from the presence of brothers and the faithfulness of God. Paul, an experienced and faithful man, still needs to feel the support of the community to move forward. It is a lesson in mutual trust and dependence on God in trials.

sens: That which provokes astonishment, admiration, or amazement
An extraordinary thing, difficult to believe or understand
G2295.detail:
1. A wonder is primarily that which seizes us with astonishment, that which leaves us speechless. It is a spectacle or event so unexpected, so remarkable, that it stuns us. Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 11:14 that Satan's transformation into an angel of light is not surprising — it is not a wonder — because it corresponds to his nature as a deceiver.

2. The word also denotes something extraordinary, a surprising reality that exceeds our ordinary expectations. John, in Revelation 17:6, is seized with astonishment upon seeing the woman drunk with the blood of the saints: this horrible and supernatural spectacle provokes in him a profound astonishment, almost a sacred stupor.
G2295.origine: The Greek word θαῦμα comes from a root that expresses the idea of looking intently, being frozen by what one sees. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew שַׂעַר (sa'ar), which also denotes horror or dread before something extraordinary. The word belongs to a rich Greek family: θαυμάζω (to be astonished), θαυμάσιος (wonderful), θαυμαστός (admirable). It is a word that paints an inner emotion — the spirit shaken by what it contemplates.
G2295.emploi: The word θαῦμα appears twice in the New Testament, each time to express an emotional reaction to the extraordinary. In 2 Corinthians 11:14, it signifies something not surprising, not remarkable (in a negative sense: "it is not a wonder"). In Revelation 17:6, it expresses John's astonishment at a supernatural vision of judgment. The usage is therefore varied: either an absence of wonder (an ordinary thing) or an authentic wonder that seizes the witness. In both cases, the word carries the idea of an emotional reaction to something that is out of the ordinary.
G2295.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian can be stunned, astonished by what surpasses him. In the face of the hidden workings of evil (Satan disguising himself) or the fearsome judgments of God, the believer's heart is shaken. It is an invitation to keep our eyes open and not to be naive in the face of the deceptive appearances of the world, while remaining awed by the majesty and justice of God.

sens: To experience surprise or astonishment at something unexpected or extraordinary
To admire something remarkable or impressive
To be struck with amazement or incomprehension in the face of an event
To examine with attention or curiosity what causes astonishment
G2296.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is the experience of surprise in the face of the unexpected. It is the feeling that seizes the shepherds upon hearing the miraculous announcement of Jesus' birth (Luke 2:18), or the crowd seeing Jesus calm the storm (Mark 5:20). Astonishment arises when reality exceeds expectations.

2. The word also expresses admiration for something beautiful or powerful. When Jesus multiplies the loaves, the crowd admires what he has done (Matthew 15:31). It is a positive astonishment, mixed with respect.

3. Sometimes astonishment borders on incredulity or scandal. The Pharisee notices with astonishment that Jesus did not wash before eating (Luke 11:38) — he is shocked by what seems contrary to the rules. Paul is astonished that the Galatians are abandoning Christ for another doctrine (Galatians 1:6).

4. The word can also denote careful observation, an inspection of the remarkable. Jesus himself is astonished at the great faith of the centurion (Matthew 8:10), paying attention to this singular behavior.
G2296.origine: The Greek verb θαυμάζω comes from the root θαῦμα, which means "wonder" or "marvel." The starting image is that of a marvel that provokes admiration and amazement. This word often translates Hebrew words related to wonder and astonishment, particularly in the face of God's acts. The Latin "mirari" (from which the French "mirer" comes) shares the same idea: to look with attention and admiration.
G2296.emploi: The verb is used 44 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and the Acts. It frequently appears to express the crowd's reaction to Jesus' miracles: they are astonished at his wisdom (Luke 4:22), at his authority over demons (Luke 11:14), at his resurrection from the dead inferred from his words (John 5:28). Jesus himself is astonished at the exceptional faith of the centurion (Matthew 8:10). In Acts, the disciples and the crowd are astonished at the miracles and the boldness of the apostles (Acts 2:7, 4:13). The verb can be intensified by an adjective ("great wonder," Revelation 17:6) and is often accompanied by complements introduced by "of," "that," "so" to specify the object of astonishment.
G2296.portee: For the reader, this word invites recognition of the extraordinary nature of God's and Christ's work. Biblical astonishment is not a mere emotional surprise, but an opening of the heart and mind before what reveals divine power and wisdom. When the crowd is astonished at Jesus' miracles, they are called to move from curiosity to faith. It is a step on the path to recognizing the Lord.

sens: Surprising due to its extraordinary nature and evokes admiration
Worthy of being contemplated with wonder
Exciting respectful fear in the presence of God's power
G2297.detail:
1. The word describes what is out of the ordinary, what astonishes and captivates the gaze: this is the effect of the miracles and wonders of Jesus. In Matthew 21:15, the wonderful things are precisely the healings and extraordinary acts that Jesus performed in the temple, which cause indignation among the religious leaders in the face of a power they cannot control.
2. Wonderful also means "worthy of admiration," something that deserves to be paused upon with wonder: this is why the children shout "Hosanna" upon seeing these acts. Their reaction springs from spontaneous amazement at a power that surpasses the human.
3. The term carries a tone of religious fear: what is wonderful reveals the presence and action of God, provoking not only admiration but also respect before the divine.
G2297.origine: The word comes from the Greek θαῦμα (thauma), which means "wonder" or "marvel." It primarily denotes what strikes the senses and provokes astonishment. In Hebrew, it often translates פָּלָא (pala), a verb meaning "to perform wonders" or "to be extraordinary." This Hebrew root evokes God's astonishing action in history: it notably appears during the miracles at the time of entering Canaan (Joshua 3:5).
G2297.emploi: The word appears only once in Greek in the New Testament (Matthew 21:15), in the neuter plural form ("the wonderful"). It denotes the extraordinary acts of Jesus: his healings, his exorcisms, his signs. In this scene in the temple, Jesus has just driven out the merchants and healed the blind and the lame. The children see these acts, recognize them as wonderful, and enthusiastically acclaim Jesus, while the religious authorities tremble with jealousy and dismay. The context shows that "wonderful" does not merely describe a subjective impression: it is a true judgment, based on the objectively extraordinary and divine nature of these works.
G2297.portee: This word calls the reader to recognize Jesus' acts for what they are: not mere historical facts or tricks, but wonders that manifest God's power and love. It invites sharing in the children's amazement rather than the skepticism or hostility of the religious leaders. To contemplate Jesus' acts as wonderful is to confess that he is God's messenger and to welcome his ministry with faith.

sens: Provoking astonishment and wonder due to its greatness or extraordinary nature
Evoking admiration and respect
Surpassing what one might expect or understand
G2298.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what strikes the mind by its marvelous and unexpected nature. It is the effect of surprise in the face of something exceptional: the stone rejected by the builders that becomes the cornerstone is "a wonder in our eyes" (Matthew 21:42), for no one would have predicted this reversal. It is astonishment in the face of the incomprehensible: the healed blind man is astonished that his interlocutors do not know where Jesus comes from, so extraordinary is what he has done (John 9:30).
2. The word then expresses respectful admiration for greatness and beauty. The elect praise God for his "admirable light" (1 Peter 2:9), that is, a light so beautiful, so pure that it deserves admiration and gratitude. The angels sing that God's works and ways are "admirable" (Revelation 15:3): it is to recognize his infinite power and wisdom.
3. The word can also simply indicate that something surprises and surpasses understanding. In Revelation 15:1, the sign of the seven angels is "great and admirable," meaning impressive and extraordinary to behold.
G2298.origine: The word comes from the verb thaumazô ("to be astonished, to admire"). It denotes what provokes this admiring astonishment. In Hebrew, the same meaning is rendered by words like pâlâ ("to be wonderful, extraordinary") and addir ("to be powerful, majestic"), hence its common use to qualify the works and ways of God in the Psalms of the Old Testament.
G2298.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, mostly in a theological context of divine revelation. In the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, John), it describes the stupefying effect produced by Jesus' acts: the resurrection of the rejected stone, the healing of the blind man. In 1 Peter and Revelation, it qualifies God's attributes and works: his light, his ways, his acts. Each time, the word emphasizes that what is admirable escapes human expectations and manifests divine power.
G2298.portee: This word reminds the believer that God often acts in ways that surprise us and exceed our understanding. The rejected stone becoming foundational, the healed blind man, the light of the Gospel: these are admirable reversals that reveal his wisdom. Recognizing God's works as admirable is to cultivate wonder before his power and humility before his unfathomable ways.

sens: A female deity, a female god in pagan mythology
The building dedicated to the worship of a goddess
G2299.detail:
1. The word refers to a female deity worshiped in Greek and Roman religion. It is simply the feminine form of "god" applied to the mythological figures that people revered as superhuman beings. In both passages from the book of Acts, it refers to Diana, the great goddess worshiped in Asia Minor: her worshipers feared that the teaching of the Gospel would ruin her cult and take away her "majesty" (Acts 19:27).
2. The word can also refer to the temple or sanctuary dedicated to a goddess. In Acts 19:35, the city clerk speaks of the "temple" of Diana, emphasizing that all of Ephesus was its guardian and drew glory and revenue from it.
G2299.origine: The word comes directly from the Greek θεός (theos), "god," with the feminine ending -ά. It is the regular feminine form, just as "god" in French has "déesse." In Hebrew from the Old Testament, the corresponding word is אֱלוֹהִים (elohim) or אלה (elah) when it refers to a female deity.
G2299.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in the account of events in Ephesus (Acts 19). In Acts 19:27, the silversmiths who made small silver temples of Diana fear that Paul's preaching will destroy the lucrative industry of the cult. In Acts 19:35, the magistrate reminds the crowd that the city of Ephesus was famous for protecting the sanctuary of this great goddess. In both cases, it is Diana (the Greek goddess of hunting and the wilderness) that is in question, and the word serves to show the contrast between false pagan religion and the true worship of the living God.
G2299.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that civilizations without the Gospel worshiped "gods" that existed only in human imagination. By seeing how the city of Ephesus was stirred to defend the worship of Diana, one measures the power of idolatry and how the preaching of the Gospel disturbs established religious structures. It is an invitation to reflect on the true nature of God and the cost of faithfulness to Christ in a hostile world.
